docs.title: Forge Fleet
docs.text:
Forge Fleet (ffleet) spins up isolated, containerized coding-agent environments — one per branch. Because each is a real git worktree, you can stack them: start a new environment from a branch that itself came from another environment's branch. It wraps the underlying moving parts (git, Docker, tmux, and the coding assistant) behind a single lifecycle and makes each environment visible and easy to reason about. Today it drives Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. Nothing forces a specific use: the work doesn't have to be complex programming, and — with --here / git-mode off — it can even run without git version control at all.

Each project's settings live in a per-project ffleet.toml written once by ffleet init (by default under the ~/.forge-fleet workdir), so you configure a project once instead of re-passing CLI flags every run — see the config reference.

  • Git options — git_mode, basing on an existing branch, local-only work, denying remote writes, commit identity.
  • Container configuration — volumes/mounts, credential dirs, extra_hosts, image selection.

  • Docker outside Docker (DooD) — using Docker from inside an environment (we do not support Docker-in-Docker).

docs.title: 0. Prerequisites & install
docs.text:
This page gets you to a working ffleet on your machine. Do it once; then head to the basic flow.

Forge Fleet runs on macOS and Linux. Windows isn't supported (WSL2 may work but is untested).

docs.title: Host prerequisites
docs.text:
Docker. Forge Fleet runs every coding-agent environment inside a Docker container, so a working Docker daemon on the host is required. Install Docker Engine (Linux) or Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) and confirm it works:

$ docker run --rm hello-world

If that prints Docker's hello message, you're set. ffleet talks to the same daemon.

Note: Forge Fleet does not use Docker-in-Docker. If you need Docker inside an environment (e.g. the agent runs docker build), that's Docker outside Docker — see docker-dood.md.

Using a non-default Docker daemon. ffleet runs the standard docker CLI and inherits its configuration, so it talks to whatever daemon your CLI does — a remote host via DOCKER_HOST, a selected docker context, or a rootless / Colima / OrbStack socket. If docker ps works in your shell, ffleet works the same way; there's no separate ffleet setting. (One exception: Docker-outside-Docker assumes a local socket at /var/run/docker.sock and won't work against a remote or non-default-path daemon.)

docs.title: Coding-assistant accounts & auth
docs.text:
Forge Fleet launches a coding assistant inside the container; it does not provide one. You need an account and working local credentials for at least one of:

  • Claude Code — Anthropic's CLI. Authenticate it on the host (e.g. log in, or run claude setup-token, or set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY). Its config/credentials live in ~/.claude.
  • OpenAI Codex — its config/credentials live in ~/.codex.

Forge Fleet mounts those host directories into the container so the agent is already authenticated inside — you don't re-login per environment. Exactly how credentials are selected and injected is covered in container-config.md and the [claude] / [codex] sections of the config reference.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The recommended way to install ffleet is via Homebrew (works on macOS and Linux):

$ brew tap grzegorz-aniol/tap
$ brew install ffleet

Then verify:

$ ffleet version
ffleet 1.x.y (commit …, built …, linux/amd64, go1.xx)

docs.title: Fallback: manual binary download
docs.text:
No Homebrew? ffleet is also distributed as a prebuilt binary from the public distribution repo:

https://github.com/grzegorz-aniol/ffleet-dist

Download the build for your platform from there, put it on your PATH (e.g. ~/.local/bin/ffleet), make it executable, and verify it the same way with ffleet version.

That repo ships binaries only — no source. It's also where you report issues (see Feedback).

docs.title: Or install with Homebrew (macOS and Linux)
docs.text:
If you use Homebrew, the tap installs and updates the same prebuilt binary for you:

$ brew install grzegorz-aniol/tap/ffleet

docs.title: Shell completion (optional, recommended)
docs.text:
Enable tab-completion for commands and options:

$ ffleet --install-completion

docs.title: Next
docs.text: You're ready. Continue to the basic flow.

docs.title: 1. Basic flow
docs.text:
The shortest route from nothing to a coding agent working in its own isolated environment. Four commands. Details come later — this page is deliberately thin.

Prerequisite: Docker running and ffleet installed (see install).

docs.title: 1. Configure the project — once
docs.text:
From inside the git repository you want to work on:

$ ffleet init

init writes an ffleet.toml for this project (by default under ~/.forge-fleet/…, so nothing needs to be committed into the repo). It runs a short wizard for the few settings worth choosing up front — coding agent, base image, git mode, and whether sandboxes get host Docker access — each pre-selected at its default, so you can press enter straight through. In a real hurry, -y accepts every default with no prompts. You only do this once per project: init is create-only and won't overwrite an existing config, so change settings later by editing the ffleet.toml it points you at (see the config reference).

docs.title: 2. Start an environment
docs.text:
$ ffleet up

Bare up creates one isolated environment — a git worktree on a fresh branch, a container, and a coding-agent session — and then attaches you to that session so you can watch and steer it. Once attached you're at a normal terminal: you type your first message to the agent yourself.

With no slug, up is interactive (it needs a terminal). If you already have environments, it lists them and asks whether to reattach to one or create a new one. If you have none, it tells you so — "No environments found; creating a new one" — and prompts for a slug to name it. It never auto-creates one silently. Say the slug you pick here is my-feature — that's the environment the rest of this walkthrough follows.

Passing -p is a variation on that same start: instead of typing your first message once attached, -p "…" / --prompt (or --prompt-file <path>) pre-types it for you, so the agent begins working as soon as the session comes up:

$ ffleet up my-feature -p "Add a --verbose flag to the CLI and cover it with tests"

You can also skip the prompts by passing things up front:

  • Give the slug on the command line: ffleet up my-feature.
  • --no-attach leaves the environment running in the background instead of attaching (--attach forces the opposite). Attaching is the default; a project can flip that with attach = false in its ffleet.toml, or an ATTACH env var — either flag still wins per run.
  • -y / --yes runs unattended: it skips the image-freshness pull prompt (it warns about a stale image but never pulls) and forces no-attach, so a scripted run can't hang on an interactive session. Pass --attach explicitly if you want to attach anyway.

Detach from an attached session any time with tmux's Ctrl-B then D — the agent keeps running. For the full set of flags, see how-to/starting.md.

docs.title: 3. Check on it
docs.text:
$ ffleet status my-feature   # is the container up? is the agent live or done?
$ ffleet tail my-feature     # last lines of the agent's transcript
$ ffleet ls                  # all environments for this project

Re-attach whenever you like by running ffleet up my-feature again — same command, no flags needed. (That's the core idea: up is state-driven — see concepts.)

docs.title: 4. Tear it down
docs.text:
When the work is merged or abandoned:

$ ffleet remove my-feature

This stops the container and deletes the worktree — and the branch too, if Forge Fleet created it. It asks first; add -y to skip the prompt.

docs.title: That's the loop
docs.text:
init once, then up → check → remove per piece of work. From here:

  • Understand the mental model → concepts.
  • Skip the typing entirely → templates. ffleet up -t task 123 fetches issue 123 from your tracker, derives the slug from its title, seeds the prompt from its fields, and can even name the subagent that works on it — steps 1–2 above from a single issue number.
  • Do more when starting → how-to/starting.md.
  • Keep a container out of the way without losing work → ffleet stop (see how-to/working.md).

docs.title: 2. Concepts
docs.text: A short shared vocabulary. Everything in the how-to guides builds on these three ideas — the slug, the scope a command acts on, and the fact that up is state-driven, not flag-driven — plus the state machine below.

docs.title: The workdir & config file
docs.text: Forge Fleet keeps its per-project state under a workdir, ~/.forge-fleet by default. Each project gets its own ffleet.toml there, written once by ffleet init, so your settings persist and you don't re-pass CLI flags on every run. Full details: config reference.

docs.title: The slug
docs.text:
Every environment has a slug: a short name you choose (e.g. my-feature, bugfix-login). It's how the environment is named and referenced — the worktree directory, the branch, and the container all derive from it, and every command takes the slug as its argument:

$ ffleet up my-feature      # start / resume it
$ ffleet status my-feature  # inspect it
$ ffleet tail my-feature    # read its transcript
$ ffleet remove my-feature  # tear it down

List the slugs you already have with ffleet ls. Pick something short and descriptive; it's the handle you'll type all day.

The branch and container are both named <project>-<slug> (e.g. project my-project + slug my-feature → my-project-my-feature) — that's the branch you push when the work is done.

Naming rules. Forge Fleet normalizes the slug (and the project name) so it's safe to use in branch, worktree, and container names:

  • trims surrounding spaces
  • trims leading/trailing - and _
  • allows only lowercase letters, digits, -, and _
  • must start and end with an alphanumeric character

If you type something that doesn't fit (e.g. mixed case or a trailing dash), it's normalized to the nearest valid form.

docs.title: Command scope
docs.text:
How much a command touches is visible in the command you type — there are no scope-widening flags to remember:

ffleet <verb> SLUG          one environment
ffleet <verb>               the current project (the one your shell is in)
ffleet projects <verb>      every project you've run `ffleet init` in

So ffleet stop my-feature parks one environment, ffleet ls lists the current project's environments (under a project: <name> header), and ffleet projects stop parks the whole machine. A verb that exists at both levels means the same thing at both — just wider.

ffleet --help therefore reads as "what acts here" and ffleet projects --help as "what acts everywhere". The projects group also owns the registry admin verbs, projects rm ID and projects prune — see completing / cleanup.

docs.title: up is state-driven, not flag-driven
docs.text:
This is the core mental model. The same command — ffleet up SLUG — does whatever the current state needs, rather than you choosing a different verb for each situation:

  • No environment yet → it creates one (worktree, branch, container, agent).
  • A live agent session → it attaches you to it.
  • A stopped container or a dead/exited agent → it rebuilds from the current config and resumes the session — without losing your work.

You don't have to remember "did I stop this? did it crash?" — you just run ffleet up SLUG and Forge Fleet reconciles reality to "running and attached". --no-attach starts it in the background (attach = false in ffleet.toml makes that the project's default, and --attach overrides it back); --peek is the strict, side-effect-free variant that attaches only if the agent is already live and never relaunches anything.

One consequence worth internalizing: on a rebuild, config-derived settings (image, mounts, hosts, env-file, auth, credential dirs, agent command/args) refresh from your current config, while identity/continuity settings (branch, worktree, git-mode, which agent, the session) stay fixed at create time. That's why some things only change after a remove — see config precedence.

docs.title: The container state machine
docs.text:
An environment moves between a handful of states. Note especially that stopped (container gone, but worktree + branch + metadata kept — revivable) is distinct from removed (worktree deleted — gone for good).

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Absent
    Absent: Absent (nothing created yet — also where ffleet remove lands)
    Running: Running (container up, agent live)
    Stopped: Stopped (container removed on purpose; worktree+branch+metadata kept)
    Interrupted: Interrupted (agent exited, setup failed, or container vanished — worktree kept)

    Absent --> Running: ffleet up SLUG
    Running --> Running: ffleet up (re-attach) · detach Ctrl-B D
    Running --> Stopped: ffleet stop
    Running --> Interrupted: agent exits · setup fails · host reboot · docker rm
    Stopped --> Running: ffleet up (revive)
    Interrupted --> Running: ffleet up (rebuild & resume)
    Running --> Absent: ffleet remove (worktree deleted — back to start)
    Stopped --> Absent: ffleet remove
    Interrupted --> Absent: ffleet remove

In prose:

  • Absent — nothing exists yet. ffleet up SLUG creates the environment. It's also where you land again after ffleet remove.
  • Running — the container is up and the agent session is live. You're either attached to it or detached (it keeps running either way).
  • Stopped — you ran ffleet stop. Because containers run with --rm, "stop" means the container is removed, but the worktree, branch, and metadata are deliberately kept. ffleet up revives it with no data loss. This is the state to leave things in when you want a container out of the way without discarding work.
  • Interrupted — the environment isn't running but its worktree is intact, whether because the agent process exited, setup failed, or the container vanished unexpectedly (host reboot, a stray docker rm, a crash). Recovery is the same in every case: ffleet up rebuilds the agent from saved metadata and resumes — no work lost. For the one cause that hits everything at once — a host or Docker restart, which takes every container with it — ffleet restore does that for all of them in one command. It only covers that case: an environment whose container is still up but whose agent died is left alone, and ffleet up SLUG is what brings it back.
  • ffleet remove — deletes the worktree (and the branch, if Forge Fleet created it). Nothing is left to revive, so the environment is back to Absent: a later ffleet up SLUG starts fresh.

The single takeaway: stop is reversible, remove is not. When in doubt, stop.

docs.title: Lifecycle at a glance
docs.text:
The everyday actions across an environment's life:

flowchart LR
    start([no environment]) -->|ffleet up SLUG -p '...'| attached[attached to agent]
    attached -->|detach: Ctrl-B D| detached[running, detached]
    detached -->|re-attach: ffleet up SLUG| attached
    start -->|background: ffleet up SLUG --no-attach| detached
    attached -->|ffleet remove SLUG| gone([removed])
    detached -->|ffleet remove SLUG| gone
  • Start: ffleet up SLUG (optionally -p to seed a prompt) — creates and attaches.
  • Detach: tmux Ctrl-B then D — leaves the agent running.
  • Re-attach: ffleet up SLUG again — same command.
  • Background start: ffleet up SLUG --no-attach — start without attaching.
  • Tear down: ffleet remove SLUG.

From here the how-to guides zoom into each stage: Starting · Working · Completing.

docs.title: Controlling the coding assistant
docs.text: Forge Fleet launches a coding assistant inside each environment's container. Which one it launches, which binary it invokes, and which flags that binary gets are all yours to shape — this page covers the knobs (--coding-agent, cmd, model, reasoning, extra_args) plus subagent selection.

docs.title: Which assistant runs
docs.text:
Forge Fleet drives Claude Code and OpenAI Codex.

$ ffleet up my-feature --coding-agent codex -p "…"
  • --coding-agent claude|codex picks it for this environment.
  • default in ffleet.toml sets the project's choice, so you don't pass the flag every time. It must name one of the [claude] / [codex] sections.
  • CODING_AGENT is the environment-variable equivalent.
  • With none of those set, ffleet launches Claude.

The choice is fixed when the environment is created. ffleet up on an existing environment ignores a different --coding-agent — switching assistants means ffleet remove SLUG and starting again.

docs.title: Per-assistant configuration
docs.text:
Each assistant has its own table in ffleet.toml:

default = "claude"

[claude]
dir       = "~/.claude"
auth      = "auto"
model     = "opus"
reasoning = "high"

[codex]
dir       = "~/.codex"
model     = "gpt-5"
reasoning = "medium"
  • dir — the host directory mounted in as the assistant's config and credentials (default ~/.claude / ~/.codex), which is why you don't re-authenticate per environment. See container configuration.
  • auth (Claude only) — which credential ffleet injects. See the [claude].auth table.
  • model — the model the assistant launches with. Omit it and the assistant picks its own default.
  • reasoning — how hard the assistant thinks by default. The same key works on both assistants; ffleet maps it onto each one's own mechanism — Claude's --effort flag, Codex's model_reasoning_effort config override.
  • cmd and extra_args — the launch command itself, below.

Both model and reasoning are opaque strings: ffleet passes them straight to the binary without checking them against a list of its own, so a value your assistant version accepts works the day it ships. Neither has a CLI flag or an environment variable — like cmd and extra_args, they are a per-project choice.

docs.title: cmd — override the binary
docs.text:
By default ffleet invokes the binary named after the section: claude or codex. cmd replaces it, which is how you run a wrapper script, a pinned version, or a binary that isn't on PATH under the expected name:

[claude]
cmd = "/usr/local/bin/claude-1.2.3"

The binary has to exist inside the container, not on your host — so a custom cmd usually goes together with a custom image.

docs.title: extra_args — your own flags
docs.text:
extra_args is a list of arguments handed to the assistant at launch. Use it for anything ffleet has no setting of its own for:

[claude]
dir = "~/.claude"
extra_args = [
    "--autocompact", "300k",
    "--permission-mode", "auto",
    "--append-system-prompt", "=== Docker here uses the HOST daemon (docker-outside-of-docker) ===",
]

[codex]
dir = "~/.codex"
extra_args = ["--search"]

Each element is one argv entry, so a flag and its value are two separate strings — ["--autocompact", "300k"], never ["--autocompact 300k"].

cmd and extra_args live in ffleet.toml only — there is no CLI flag and no environment variable for either, so they are a per-project choice rather than a per-run one. For the model and reasoning effort, prefer the dedicated keys above over hand-written flags here.

docs.title: Where your flags land in the command
docs.text:
Your extra_args go immediately after the binary, before every flag ffleet adds for itself — with model and reasoning, when set, just ahead of them. For Claude the assembled command is:

<cmd> [--model <model>] [--effort <reasoning>] <extra_args…> --dangerously-skip-permissions -n <env-name> --session-id <uuid> [prompt]

and on a revive --session-id <uuid> becomes --resume <uuid> — unless ffleet finds no transcript for that session on the host, in which case it keeps --session-id <uuid> and the session starts fresh under the same id. Codex follows the same shape, with reasoning as a config override rather than a flag:

<cmd> [--model <model>] [-c model_reasoning_effort=<reasoning>] <extra_args…> -c check_for_update_on_startup=false …

With a prompt the rest is exec, resume --last when reviving, --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox and the prompt; without one Codex stays interactive and it is just --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox followed by resume --last when reviving.

Three consequences follow from that order:

  • ffleet's own flags win a last-one-wins duel. For a flag where the last occurrence takes effect, putting the same flag in extra_args will not override ffleet's value. The flags ffleet sets are the ones it needs to run the assistant unattended and to resume the right session, so this is deliberate.
  • -n is the one exception. ffleet names the Claude session after the environment so /resume, the terminal title and the Remote Control list identify it — but if your extra_args already carry -n, --name or --name=…, ffleet leaves the name alone and adds nothing.
  • extra_args wins over model / reasoning. Those two come first, so a --model you write in extra_args yourself is the later occurrence and takes effect. Set the key, or write the flag by hand — not both.

--append-system-prompt is merged rather than duplicated: when ffleet has environment notes to add (see [claude].extend_system_prompt) they end up in a single flag with ffleet's text first and yours last.

docs.title: Subagents
docs.text:
A subagent is a named agent definition the assistant itself resolves — a reviewer, a test-writer, a domain specialist. Forge Fleet can launch an environment straight into one, on both claude and codex, though the two work quite differently under the hood:

$ ffleet up my-feature --subagent code-reviewer -p "Review the diff on this branch"

A template can carry the same choice, so environments seeded from it always run the right subagent:

[templates.review]
prompt_template = "Review issue #{number}: {title}"
subagent = "code-reviewer"

--subagent works with or without -t/--template, and when both are set the flag wins — ffleet warns when the two disagree. See templates for the rest of the template machinery.

--subagent is a create-time flag on both agents: on an ffleet up that revives an existing environment it is ignored outright.

docs.title: Claude — a deterministic flag
docs.text:
--subagent NAME is translated into Claude's own --agent NAME and appended to extra_args, so it reaches the binary exactly as if you had written it there yourself. That flag is what carries the choice forward — the subagent has no stored setting of its own.

That has a consequence worth planning for: extra_args is re-read from your config on every revive, and the saved list is used only when your config supplies no extra_args at all. So an environment created with --subagent in a project that also sets [claude].extra_args loses its subagent on the next stop + up — the configured list replaces the saved one rather than merging with it. If you need both, write the pair into your own extra_args and drop the flag:

[claude]
extra_args = ["--agent", "code-reviewer"]

docs.title: Codex — a best-effort delegation instruction
docs.text:
The Codex CLI has no --agent-equivalent flag, so ffleet cannot make Codex adopt a subagent the way it can Claude. Instead, at create time only, ffleet:

  1. looks up NAME in ~/.codex/agents/*.toml (personal) and .codex/agents/*.toml in the repo (project) — matched on the file's name field, not the filename; a duplicate or missing name is a fail-fast error, not a silent fallback;
  2. weaves a delegation instruction naming that agent into the launch prompt (-p "…"), or, for an interactive launch with no prompt, sends the same instruction into the pane right after Codex comes up.

Codex decides for itself whether to follow that instruction — there is no enforcement — so treat --subagent on Codex as a strong hint, not a guarantee the way it is on Claude. Nothing is written into extra_args or saved with the environment, so there is nothing to carry forward on revive even in principle: it applies once, at the moment of creation.

docs.title: What a stop + up picks up
docs.text:
cmd, model, reasoning and extra_args are config-derived: they are re-read from your config on every ffleet up and saved back, so changing them takes effect on the next revive.

$ ffleet stop my-feature
$ ffleet up my-feature      # relaunches with the new cmd / model / reasoning / extra_args

The section re-read is the environment's own assistant's — [claude] for an environment running Claude, [codex] for one running Codex — regardless of what --coding-agent, CODING_AGENT or your project default say when you type ffleet up. For an environment whose assistant differs from that default, its own section is authoritative: ffleet prints a warning, applies that section, and replaces whatever cmd/extra_args were saved with the environment — so if your config configures none for it, it revives with none.

The assistant is an identity setting instead — pinned when the environment is created, changeable only by removing it and starting fresh. The subagent is never stored separately either, but the two agents get there differently: on Claude it rides along inside extra_args, so it follows the config-derived rule above; on Codex it isn't stored at all — it's a one-time instruction applied only at creation (see the subagents section). See config precedence for the full split.

docs.title: Config precedence
docs.text: When a setting could come from more than one place, Forge Fleet resolves it in a fixed order. Understanding this explains two things that surprise people: why a flag sometimes "wins" over your config, and why some settings only take effect after a remove.

docs.title: The order (highest wins)
docs.text:
1. CLI flag — e.g. --image, --git-mode, -p. Explicit on the command line; applies to this run.
  2. Environment variable / dotenv — e.g. IMAGE_NAME, GIT_MODE, or an entry in .env.forge-fleet / .forge-fleet/.env. See the env-var mapping.
  3. ffleet.toml — the project's configured value.
  4. Built-in default — what ffleet uses when none of the above is set (e.g. image = forge-fleet:latest, git_mode = auto, wait-timeout = 300).

So a flag overrides an env var / dotenv entry, which overrides the config file, which overrides the default. Nothing exotic — the twist is when the resolved value gets applied.

docs.title: Identity is config-only
docs.text: The precedence order above applies to shape settings (--image, mounts, hosts, git-mode, and so on). An environment's identity — project_name, source_dir, worktree_root — is different: it is read only from ffleet.toml, with no CLI-flag or environment-variable override. There is no --project-name / --source-dir / --worktree-root flag and no PROJECT_NAME / SOURCE_DIR / WORKTREE_ROOT env-var bridge. Run ffleet init to create the config; the env commands (up, remove, ls, status, …) fail with no ffleet config found — run 'ffleet init' until one exists.

docs.title: Why some settings only apply after remove
docs.text:
An environment's settings split into two groups, and ffleet up treats them differently on a revive/rebuild (this is stated in ffleet up --help):

  • Config-derived (refreshed every up) — image, extra_mounts, extra_hosts, docker_env_file, credential auth, credential dirs (~/.claude / ~/.codex), agent cmd / model / reasoning / extra_args. These are re-read from your current config/flags each time and saved back. Change one, then ffleet stop SLUG + ffleet up SLUG to apply it.
  • Identity/continuity (fixed at create) — branch, worktree, in-place vs worktree mode, git-mode, which coding agent, and the session. These are pinned when the environment is first created and do not change on revive, because changing them would mean a different environment. To change one you must ffleet remove SLUG and recreate.
flowchart TD
    F[CLI flag] --> R{resolve}
    E[env var / dotenv] --> R
    T[ffleet.toml] --> R
    D[built-in default] --> R
    R --> V[effective value for this run]
    V --> K{which kind of setting?}
    K -->|config-derived| RE[applied now; refreshed on every up]
    K -->|identity/continuity| FX[fixed at create; needs remove to change]

docs.title: Practical rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Passed a flag and it did what you expected → good, flags are top of the order.
  • Changed image/mounts/env-file and want it live → stop then up.
  • Need a different branch, git-mode, or agent → remove and start fresh; there's no in-place way to change identity.
  • Not sure which bucket a setting is in → check the table in how-to/working.md.

docs.title: How the container is configured
docs.text: Each environment is a Docker container that Forge Fleet assembles from your ffleet.toml and flags. This page explains the pieces so you can tune them.

docs.title: Image
docs.text:
image (or --image) selects the Docker image the agent runs in. Default: ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-python:latest (pulled from GHCR on first use — no local build required). A Go-dev variant (ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-go:latest, also published to GHCR) overlays a Go toolchain for developing the Go port. Pick or build an image that carries the language runtimes and tools your project needs — the agent can only use what's in the image (plus what it installs at runtime).

Because image is a config-derived setting, you can change it and pick it up on the next revive: ffleet stop SLUG then ffleet up SLUG (see what can change mid-life).

docs.title: How the published images are built
docs.text:
The two default images are built and pushed to GHCR from the public ffleet-dist repo (its publish-images workflow), where the Dockerfiles live:

  • ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-python:latest — the base image (Debian bookworm-slim). It carries the agent toolbox: the Claude Code and Codex CLIs, Python 3 + uv, Node 22 (with corepack for pnpm/yarn), plus git, gh (GitHub CLI), the docker CLI (client only, for DooD), tmux, jq, make, and a C build toolchain.
  • ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-go:latest — a superset overlay of the base that adds the Go toolchain (for developing the Go port); the rest of the toolbox is identical.

Each is published multi-arch (linux/amd64 + linux/arm64), so Apple Silicon Macs pull and run a native image without emulation.

Both run as a non-root user buddy (uid/gid 1000) with home /home/buddy, and the workspace directory is owned by buddy. That is why credential and cache mounts land under /home/buddy/... (e.g. ~/.claude → /home/buddy/.claude), why extra_mounts into the container home use that path, and why host Docker access adds buddy to the host docker group so it can reach the socket (see DooD). If you build a custom image, matching the buddy uid/gid 1000 keeps mounted-file ownership aligned with your host user.

docs.title: Volumes & mounts
docs.text:
Several things get mounted into the container:

  • The workspace — the git worktree (or, in --here/off mode, your current directory) is mounted into the container at its host-identical absolute path (e.g. /srv/worktrees/creator-ai/creator-ai-feat1), not a fixed /workspace. This is where the agent does its work; it also gives every environment a unique container cwd, which matters for Codex session resume (see below).
  • uv_cache_dir — a shared uv cache (default ~/.cache/uv) for faster Python installs across environments.
  • extra_mounts — your own bind mounts.

docs.title: extra_mounts — your own bind mounts
docs.text:
Each entry is source:target[:ro|:rw]. The target is an absolute container path; the source is a host path that must already exist — ffleet resolves it before starting the container and fails with the resolved path if it doesn't.

extra_mounts = [
    # Read-only reference material the agent should read but never edit.
    "~/notes/architecture:/home/buddy/architecture:ro",

    # Read-write shared cache, so every environment reuses one Go module cache.
    "~/.cache/go-build:/home/buddy/.cache/go-build:rw",

    # `rw` is the default — this line means the same as the one above.
    "~/.cache/go-build:/home/buddy/.cache/go-build",

    # A relative source resolves against the shell's cwd when `ffleet up` runs.
    "fixtures/large-dataset:/home/buddy/dataset:ro",
]

Things worth knowing:

  • ro and rw are the only accepted modes, and the default is read-write. Anything else (z, delegated, cached) is rejected. Reach for :ro whenever the agent has no business writing to the host path — it is the cheapest way to stop an agent editing your real files.
  • ~ expands to your host home, which keeps a source portable across machines. A relative source, by contrast, is resolved against the shell's current directory at the moment you run ffleet up — not against the repo root — so the same entry breaks when you launch from a different subdirectory. Prefer absolute or ~-relative sources; keep relative ones only for a directory you always launch from.
  • The container runs as buddy (uid/gid 1000), so mounts meant for the agent's home belong under /home/buddy/.... A host directory owned by a different uid will be read-only in practice regardless of the mode you ask for.
  • Shadowing works, exact duplicates don't. A target nested inside an existing mount is layered on top of it, leaving the rest of that mount intact — so "~/shared-agents:/home/buddy/.claude/agents:ro" shares one set of agent definitions across projects without disturbing the rest of the mounted ~/.claude. Targeting the exact path of a built-in mount (/home/buddy/.claude itself, the workspace root, the uv cache) instead makes Docker refuse to start the container with a duplicate-mount-point error; change those through their own settings ([claude].dir, uv_cache_dir).
  • ffleet up prints every resolved mount — extras and built-ins — while starting, which is the quickest way to check what actually landed where.

See secrets for when to mount vs. copy vs. env-file; a mount is the right answer when the container should see a host path live and as-is.

docs.title: Credential directories — authenticating the agent inside
docs.text:
The agent must be logged in inside the container. Forge Fleet handles this by mounting the agent's host credential/config directory:

  • Claude Code — [claude].dir (default ~/.claude), plus a credential auth source (auto / keychain / token / api-key / credentials-file / external) that decides which credential ffleet injects. See the [claude].auth table.
  • Codex — [codex].dir (default ~/.codex).

Override the mounts per run with --claude-dir / --codex-dir, and the Claude source with --claude-auth. The upshot: because your host login is mounted in, you don't re-authenticate per environment.

Codex resumes the most recently used session within its cwd filter, not by ID. Unlike Claude, the Codex CLI has no way to resume a specific session by an externally chosen ID — ffleet up on a stopped Codex environment runs codex resume --last, which (per Codex's own documentation for its --all flag) filters candidate sessions down to the ones started from the same working directory. Because each environment's container workspace is always mounted at its own host-identical path (see "Volumes & mounts" above), concurrent Codex environments get distinct cwds even though they share [codex].dir by default — so --last resolves to the right environment's session in the common case. This isn't an absolute guarantee for every possible setup, so if you ever see a Codex environment resume the wrong session, giving that environment its own --codex-dir removes the ambiguity entirely.

docs.title: extra_hosts
docs.text:
extra_hosts maps hostnames to addresses via docker run --add-host, letting processes inside resolve names to the host or to arbitrary addresses. Each entry is host:address; the special value host-gateway resolves to the host itself — handy for reaching a service running on your machine:

extra_hosts = ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]

docs.title: Reaching a service on your host (e.g. an MCP server)
docs.text:
A common case: the agent needs to reach something running on your host — an MCP server, a local API, a dev database. Two pieces must line up:

  1. Give the container a name for the host. Map host.docker.internal to the host gateway:
extra_hosts = ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]

Then point the agent at host.docker.internal:<port> (e.g. in your Claude MCP config under the mounted ~/.claude). 2. Bind the host service so the container can reach it. host-gateway reaches your host on its bridge interface, not its loopback — a service bound only to 127.0.0.1 on the host is unreachable from the container. Bind it to 0.0.0.0 (or the docker bridge address) instead.

Editing your host's /etc/hosts doesn't help here: it only changes name resolution on the host, not inside the container (which has its own /etc/hosts). The container-side mapping is exactly what extra_hosts provides.

docs.title: Pointing a hostname at a fixed address
docs.text:
An address other than host-gateway is taken literally, which lets you pin a name the container would otherwise fail to resolve — an internal service on your VPN, or a staging host you want the agent's tests to hit:

extra_hosts = [
    "host.docker.internal:host-gateway",
    "api.internal.example.com:10.0.3.14",
    "staging.example.com:203.0.113.7",
]

Entries are independent, so mix host-gateway and literal addresses freely. This only maps names to addresses — the container still needs a network route to reach them, so a VPN-only address works from a container only if the host routes that range.

docs.title: Host Docker access
docs.text: docker_host_bind = true (or --docker-host-bind) binds the host Docker socket so the agent can drive the host daemon — this is the Docker-outside-Docker setup; see DooD.

docs.title: Git inside the container
docs.text:
The container gets no SSH key and no host git config. Its init script instead rewrites git remotes to HTTPS in the container's own gitconfig (url."https://<host>/".insteadOf "git@<host>:", host taken from your origin), so the agent only needs a token — see git push credentials. The repository's own git config is never modified. It also stamps in a commit identity, without which the container refuses to start.

Both of those, along with git_mode, --from and denying the agent remote writes, are covered in git options.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
image = "ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-python:latest"
uv_cache_dir = "~/.cache/uv"
extra_mounts = ["~/.agents:/home/buddy/.agents"]
extra_hosts  = ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]

[claude]
dir  = "~/.claude"
# auth = "auto"

[git]
user_name  = "Jane Developer"
user_email = "jane@example.com"

docs.title: Docker outside Docker (DooD)
docs.text: Sometimes the agent needs Docker inside its environment — to run docker build, spin up a test database, or run integration tests in containers. Forge Fleet supports this, but not the way people often assume.

docs.title: We do not do Docker-in-Docker
docs.text: Docker-in-Docker (DinD) runs a second, nested Docker daemon inside the container. It's heavy, needs privileged mode, and is fiddly to get right. Forge Fleet does not use it.

docs.title: We do Docker outside Docker (DooD)
docs.text:
Docker-outside-of-Docker (DooD) instead lets the agent's container talk to the host's Docker daemon — the same one ffleet itself uses. There's no nested daemon: the Docker CLI inside the environment is just a client pointed at the host socket. Containers the agent starts are therefore siblings of the agent's container (both children of the host daemon), not children nested inside it.

flowchart TD
    subgraph host[Host]
        D[Host Docker daemon]
        D --> AC[Agent container]
        D --> SC[Sibling container the agent started]
        AC -. docker CLI over host socket .-> D
    end

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
Set the host-bind option, which binds the host Docker socket into the agent container:

  • Config: docker_host_bind = true in ffleet.toml.
  • Or per run: ffleet up SLUG --docker-host-bind ….

With that on, docker … commands run by the agent are executed by the host daemon.

docs.title: What the agent is told
docs.text:
DooD is unusual enough that an agent can easily assume the wrong model — that its docker run nests containers inside its own, or resolves bind mounts against its own filesystem. So when the host bind is on and the agent is Claude, ffleet appends one short sentence to its system prompt: that this environment runs Docker in docker-outside-of-docker mode, where the docker CLI talks to the host daemon and started containers are siblings rather than nested.

It is merged with any --append-system-prompt of your own in [claude].extra_args (yours is kept, and comes last), and recomputed at each launch. To turn it off, set extend_system_prompt = false in the [claude] section.

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• Shared daemon = shared blast radius. The agent can see and affect the host's other containers, images, and volumes. Only enable DooD for environments you trust to drive Docker.
  • Paths are host paths. Because the real daemon is the host's, any bind mount the agent's docker run requests is resolved on the host filesystem, not inside the agent container. Mount host paths the agent can actually reach — see container configuration and extra_mounts.
  • Sibling lifetime. Containers the agent starts are independent siblings; they don't get cleaned up automatically when the environment is stopped or removed. The agent (or you) should tear them down.

docs.text:

docs.title: Git options
docs.text: Every environment gets its own git setup, and a handful of settings decide what that setup looks like: whether git is involved at all, what the branch is based on, whether the agent may publish, and whose name ends up on the commits. This page walks through them in the order you'll meet them. The exhaustive key list lives in the config reference.

docs.title: git_mode — how git is wired up
docs.text:
--git-mode auto|worktree|off|clone (config key git_mode, env var GIT_MODE; default auto).

  • worktree — the isolated default. Forge Fleet creates a git worktree on a fresh branch off your source repo and mounts it into the container. Your main checkout is never touched, and environments can be stacked: start a new one from a branch that itself came from another environment.
  • off — no git integration at all. The agent works directly in the mounted directory: no worktree, no branch, and no git repository required. This is how you point Forge Fleet at a plain folder — notes, a data directory, a scratch project.
  • auto — resolves to worktree in a normal repo, and falls back to off when there's nothing to branch from: no git repo, or a directory that is the repository's primary checkout rather than a linked worktree.
  • clone — reserved, not implemented yet. The value passes validation but the container's init script rejects it, so the environment fails to start. Use worktree or auto.
$ ffleet up my-feature --git-mode worktree     # explicit isolation
$ cd ~/notes && ffleet up braindump --here     # in-place, no worktree

--here is the per-run form of off: it starts an agent over your current directory. Setting git_mode = "off" makes that the project's default and points it at the project root from any subdirectory, so you don't pass --here each time.

git_mode is an identity setting — pinned when the environment is created. Changing it means ffleet remove SLUG and starting again.

docs.title: Choosing what the branch is based on
docs.text:
By default a new worktree's branch forks from your remote's default branch: ffleet fetches, then takes the first of origin/HEAD, origin/main, local main, origin/master, local master, HEAD that resolves.

--from BRANCH overrides that for a first-time worktree — base the work on an existing branch instead of the default one:

$ ffleet up hotfix --from release-2.3 -p "Cherry-pick the logging fix"

It's ignored once the environment exists (the branch is already created), and a branch you brought in with --from is left alone by ffleet remove — only branches Forge Fleet created itself get deleted.

docs.title: git_local_main — stay off the network
docs.text:
--git-local-main (config key git_local_main, env var GIT_LOCAL_MAIN; default false) bases the branch on your local refs/heads/main and nothing else — if that ref doesn't exist, the environment fails rather than quietly falling back to a remote branch.

git_local_main = true

Use it when the work should stay local: you merge on your own machine, with no push and no PR. It pairs naturally with git_allow_origin_writes = false below, but neither implies the other — set both for a genuinely local-only environment.

docs.title: git_allow_origin_writes — let the agent commit but not publish
docs.text:
git_allow_origin_writes (env var GIT_ALLOW_ORIGIN_WRITES; default true, no CLI flag). Agents inside the container run with their own approval prompts disabled, so once push credentials are present nothing but the agent's judgement stops it publishing work you haven't reviewed. Setting it to false denies the outward-facing commands at the agent's own permission layer:

git_allow_origin_writes = false

git push · gh pr create · gh pr merge · gh release create · gh workflow run · gh api with a mutating method

The agent can still commit locally; it just cannot publish. Matching is by command prefix, so the coverage has real edges — read the caveats before you rely on it. It raises the bar; it is not a sandbox.

It is sticky per environment. Once an environment has been created or started with a value, later starts keep it even if you delete the key from ffleet.toml — dropping the line does not quietly re-open remote writes. To re-enable them, set git_allow_origin_writes = true explicitly; an explicit value always wins.

docs.title: Push credentials and git_https_rewrite
docs.text:
The container gets no SSH key and no host git config, so it has no push auth until you give it some. What it does have is an HTTPS transport: at every start the init script writes a rewrite into the container's own gitconfig, derived from your origin host —

[url "https://github.com/"]
    insteadOf = git@github.com:
    insteadOf = ssh://git@github.com/

— so an SSH origin URL still fetches and pushes with nothing but a token. The repository's git config is never modified; it is shared with your host and every other environment.

Supply the token as a fine-grained personal access token scoped to that one repository, through docker_env_file. Prefer that to mounting ~/.ssh: a mounted key is your real, long-lived credential, valid everywhere it can reach for as long as the environment lives.

git_https_rewrite = false (env var GIT_HTTPS_REWRITE; default true, no CLI flag) turns the rewrite off — for example when you deliberately mount your own SSH agent socket. Unlike git_allow_origin_writes it is not sticky: every start re-reads it from your config.

docs.title: Commit identity
docs.text:
Commits made inside the container need a user.name / user.email. Set a project-specific pair in ffleet.toml:

[git]
user_name  = "Jane Developer"
user_email = "jane@example.com"

Those two keys are bridged into FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_NAME / FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_EMAIL, which is also where a shell or dotenv value lands — and an already-set variable wins, so the environment overrides the config file. From there Forge Fleet takes the first complete pair:

  1. FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_NAME + FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_EMAIL — from [git], your shell, or .env.forge-fleet.
  2. The identity recorded for this environment when it was created, so a revived environment keeps signing commits the way it always has.
  3. Your source repository's git config.
  4. Your global git config.

If none of them yields a pair, ffleet up fails and tells you to set the variables or configure git — the container never starts without an identity.

Both or neither. Half a pair is not a partial override: setting exactly one of the two variables — including a [git] table with only user_name — is a hard error rather than a fall-through to the next source.

docs.title: Environment-variable equivalents
docs.text:
Every git setting has a dotenv/env-var form, useful for a machine-specific value you don't want in a shared ffleet.toml:

# .env.forge-fleet
GIT_MODE=worktree
GIT_LOCAL_MAIN=false
GIT_ALLOW_ORIGIN_WRITES=false
GIT_HTTPS_REWRITE=true
FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_NAME=Jane Developer
FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_EMAIL=jane@example.com

A CLI flag beats an env var, which beats ffleet.toml, which beats the default — see config precedence.

docs.title: Secrets & keys
docs.text:
Agents often need secrets inside the environment — API keys, tokens, a project .env. Forge Fleet gives you three mechanisms, each suited to a different shape of secret. Pick by what the secret is and how the code expects to read it.

Mechanism Config key Secret arrives as Best for Env file docker_env_file Environment variables in the container API keys/tokens the process reads from the environment (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, LINEAR_API_KEY, DB URLs) File snapshot copy_files A copy of a file placed in the worktree A project .env / local config file the app loads from disk Bind mount extra_mounts A live-mounted host path in the container Directories you want shared as-is (e.g. a shared cache, ~/.agents)

docs.title: 1. docker_env_file — inject environment variables
docs.text:
Point at an env file; its KEY=value lines are passed to the container via docker run --env-file, so they're present as environment variables for every process inside.

# A relative path resolves against this config file's own directory.
docker_env_file = "docker.env"

$ ffleet up SLUG --docker-env-file ./docker.env

# docker.env
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-…
LINEAR_API_KEY=lin_api_…
DATABASE_URL=postgres://…

Use this for runtime secrets read from the environment. It's also the natural home for LINEAR_API_KEY when using Linear templates, and the companion to [claude].auth = "external", where you supply credentials yourself instead of letting ffleet's preflight find them.

The env file itself lives on the host and is never committed into the repo — keep it out of version control.

docs.title: 2. copy_files — snapshot a file into the worktree
docs.text:
Some apps don't read the environment; they load a file from disk (a .env, a config/local.json). copy_files snapshots gitignored files from your main checkout into each new worktree, at the same relative path.

copy_files = [".env", "config/local.json"]

Key properties:

  • One-time copy at creation, not a live link — later edits on either side don't sync.
  • The agent works on the copy, so it can't clobber your real file.
  • Entries are relative to the main checkout; globs are allowed.

Prefer this over a mount for env/local-config files. Inside the container the file appears at the same relative path inside the workspace (e.g. .env at the workspace root).

docs.title: 3. extra_mounts — bind-mount a host path
docs.text:
When you want the container to see a host directory or credential as-is, mount it. This is a live bind mount, not a copy.

extra_mounts = [
  "~/.agents:/home/buddy/.agents",
  "~/.cache/pip:/home/buddy/.cache/pip",
]

Format is source:target[:mode]: the target must be an absolute container path, ~ expands to the host home, and a relative source resolves against the shell's current directory when ffleet up runs — so prefer absolute or ~-relative sources. Use this for shared caches and tool directories — anything you want shared and kept in sync, accepting that the container has live access to the real path.

Don't mount ~/.ssh. Earlier versions of this guide suggested ~/.ssh:/home/buddy/.ssh as the way to give an agent push access. That mount hands the sandbox your real, long-lived private key: usable against every host and repository that key is authorized for, for as long as the environment exists — not scoped to one repo, one session, or one operation. Use the token recipe below instead.

docs.title: Git push credentials
docs.text:
Agent containers get no SSH key. Instead, the container rewrites git remotes to HTTPS in its own gitconfig — see git_https_rewrite — so all it needs is a token in the environment:

  1. Create a fine-grained personal access token scoped to the single repository, with only the permissions the agent needs (for GitHub: Contents: Read and write, plus Pull requests: Read and write if it opens PRs). Give it a short expiry.
  2. Put it in the env file you already pass with docker_env_file:
# docker.env
GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_…
GH_TOKEN=github_pat_…

gh picks up GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN directly, and gh auth setup-git (run inside the container) makes plain git push use it too.

Unlike a mounted key, this credential is limited to one repository, carries only the permissions you granted, and expires. Revoking it is a single click and does not touch anything else you own.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:
• The value is a credential the process reads from the environment → env file.
  • It's a file the app loads from disk, and the agent shouldn't touch your original → copy_files.
  • It's a directory you want shared live, edits included → extra_mounts.
  • It's push access to your repo → a repo-scoped fine-grained token in the env file, never a mounted SSH key.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: Templates turn a tracked issue into a ready-to-go environment: ffleet up -t <id> <ref> fetches the issue from your project-management (PM) tool, derives the slug from its title, and seeds the agent with a prompt rendered from the issue's fields. It's the fastest way to say "go work on ticket 123".

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
A template is a [templates.<id>] table in ffleet.toml plus a pm setting that says where issues come from.

# Where -t templates fetch issues from: github | linear | none
pm = "github"

[templates.task]
prompt_template = """
Work on issue #{number}: {title}

{body}

Issue URL: {url}
"""
# Optional: run a specific subagent for envs seeded from this template.
# subagent = "code-reviewer"

docs.title: Available fields
docs.text:
prompt_template is rendered with the fetched issue's fields:

Token Value {number} Issue number {title} Issue title {body} Issue body {url} Issue URL {id} The raw <ref> you passed

You can add or override tokens inline as key=value on the command line — e.g. ffleet up -t task 100 priority=high makes {priority} available in the template.

docs.title: Running a template
docs.text:
The SLUG argument becomes the template ref (usually the issue id):

$ ffleet up -t task 123

Forge Fleet fetches issue 123 via the configured pm, derives a slug from its title, renders the prompt, and starts the environment just like a normal ffleet up. From there everything is the same — attach, stop, remove, etc.

The optional subagent key selects a subagent for these envs. On Claude, it's translated to a deterministic --agent <name> flag. On Codex, it's a best-effort delegation instruction (Codex has no equivalent flag) — see starting for how that works. Using it with any other coding-agent errors.

The --subagent NAME CLI flag (see starting) is the per-invocation, template-independent equivalent — it works with or without -t. When both are set, --subagent always wins over the template's configured subagent; if the two differ, Forge Fleet prints a non-fatal warning and proceeds with the CLI value. Passing a matching value, or passing only one of the two, produces no warning.

docs.title: PM-tool integration
docs.text:
The pm setting controls fetching:

pm How issues are fetched Requirements github (default) Via the gh CLI gh installed and authenticated linear Via the Linear API LINEAR_API_KEY (e.g. in an env file — see secrets); refs may be a UUID or a human id like ENG-123 none No fetch; the raw <ref> is exposed as {id} —

On any fetch failure, Forge Fleet warns and continues as if pm = none, so a transient outage won't block you — you just get the raw ref instead of the issue fields.

docs.title: GitHub example
docs.text:
pm = "github"

[templates.bug]
prompt_template = """
Fix bug #{number}: {title}

{body}

{url}
"""

$ ffleet up -t bug 456

docs.title: Linear example
docs.text:
Put LINEAR_API_KEY in your project's env file (see secrets), then:

pm = "linear"

[templates.task]
prompt_template = "Implement {title} ({id}):\n\n{body}\n\n{url}"

$ ffleet up -t task ENG-123
