docs.title: Troubleshooting & recovery
docs.text:
Most problems fall into one loop: diagnose with status / tail, recover with stop + up. Because stop keeps the worktree, branch, and metadata, you can rebuild a broken container without losing any work.

flowchart TD
    P[Something's wrong] --> S[ffleet status SLUG]
    S --> T[ffleet tail SLUG]
    T --> D{What is it?}
    D -->|agent exited / container broken| R[ffleet stop SLUG → ffleet up SLUG]
    D -->|config change needed| C[edit ffleet.toml → stop → up]
    D -->|identity change needed| X[ffleet remove SLUG → ffleet up SLUG …]
    R --> OK[Running again, work preserved]
    C --> OK

docs.title: Step 1: diagnose
docs.text:
• ffleet status SLUG — is the container up? is the agent live or exited? is it still working or done with its turn? This is the first look.
  • ffleet tail SLUG — the last lines of the agent's transcript (--lines N for more). Shows what the agent was doing or the error it hit.
  • ffleet ls — confirm the environment exists and its overall state.

docs.title: The agent crashed or the container is broken
docs.text:
Rebuild it from saved config — your worktree and session survive:

$ ffleet stop my-feature   # remove the broken container (keeps everything else)
$ ffleet up   my-feature   # rebuild from config, resume the session

Often you can skip straight to ffleet up my-feature — up detects a dead agent or a missing container and rebuilds. Use the explicit stop first when you want a guaranteed-clean container.

docs.title: up fails with "agent exited immediately after launch"
docs.text:
The agent started but died within the first seconds, so Forge Fleet fails the command instead of reporting a resumed environment you cannot attach to. The agent's own last output is printed with the error — that line is the real cause, e.g. No conversation found with session ID: … (the saved session is gone from the container) or an authentication complaint.

Fix what that line points at, then rebuild:

$ ffleet stop my-feature   # remove the container (keeps worktree and config)
$ ffleet up   my-feature

If the container is still up, ffleet tail my-feature shows the agent's recent output. When a failed launch also tore the container down, the error text you already have is all there was.

A rebuild only helps when the container was the problem. A saved session the agent can no longer find survives it: up resumes the same session id and fails the same way. Forge Fleet has no in-place repair for that — tear the environment down and create it again:

$ ffleet remove my-feature   # also deletes the worktree and, if ffleet created it, the branch
$ ffleet up     my-feature   # absent env -> created fresh, with a new session

Commit and push anything in the worktree you want to keep before removing it.

docs.title: An environment sits at RUNTIME failed
docs.text:
failed means the container is up but its agent never appeared — the launch died somewhere between starting the container and starting the agent. ffleet status says the same in agent terms: agent state: exited, probe reason: agent exited.

$ ffleet tail my-feature   # anything the agent managed to write before dying
$ ffleet up   my-feature   # relaunch the agent in the running container

If up lands back at failed, rebuild the container as above (stop + up).

A starting environment is not this case — it is still inside its launch window (the first two minutes) and should reach running in a few seconds.

docs.title: Everything is gone after a reboot or a Docker restart
docs.text:
Containers don't survive a host restart or a Docker daemon restart — but your worktrees, branches and saved sessions do. Bring the agents back in one go:

$ ffleet projects restore  # every project; plain `ffleet restore` for just this one

It revives only the environments that were supposed to be running (anything you parked with ffleet stop stays parked), sends no message and attaches nothing, and is safe to re-run. See Working / restore.

docs.title: A config change isn't taking effect
docs.text:
If you changed image, a mount, hosts, or the env file and don't see it, revive to refresh config-derived settings:

$ ffleet stop my-feature && ffleet up my-feature

If the setting you changed is an identity setting (branch, git-mode, agent, worktree mode), a revive won't pick it up — you must recreate:

$ ffleet remove my-feature      # deletes worktree + ffleet-created branch — check for unpushed work!
$ ffleet up my-feature --git-mode … …

remove warns when the worktree still holds uncommitted changes or untracked files, or commits that no remote branch contains. It reads only your local remote-tracking refs (origin/…) and never fetches, so it stays fast and works offline — but if those refs are stale, it can warn about commits you have already pushed. Run git fetch --prune and re-check when a warning looks wrong.

See config precedence for which bucket a setting is in.

docs.title: A directory named ~ appeared inside a worktree
docs.text:
Symptom. A worktree contains a literal ~ directory, usually holding .cache/uv.

Cause. Older Forge Fleet versions exported UV_CACHE_DIR verbatim, so a config or dotenv value like ~/.cache/uv reached the shell started by ffleet goto unexpanded. uv then treated it as a relative path and created the cache under the current directory. Current versions expand ~ before exporting the variable, so upgrading fixes it.

Fix. Upgrade Forge Fleet, then delete the stray directory — keep the quotes, an unquoted ~ would target your home directory:

$ rm -rf '/path/to/worktree/~'

Any ffleet goto shell you already have open still carries the old value: exit and re-enter it.

docs.title: Environment shows as broken (worktree registration missing)
docs.text:
Symptom. ffleet ls still lists the environment but prints a warning under the table, and ffleet status SLUG shows a broken: field:

$ ffleet ls
...
Warning: broken environment(s):
  - my-project-my-feature: worktree_registration_missing
  Git no longer works inside them. Never run `git worktree prune` inside a container; see the troubleshooting guide to recover.

Inside the container, git commands fail with something like fatal: not a git repository.

Cause. Someone ran git worktree prune inside a container (an agent "cleaning up" counts). In worktree git mode every environment mounts the host repository's shared .git directory, and that directory holds the registration of every worktree — your other environments included. From inside a container the sibling worktrees are not mounted, so git considers them gone and prunes their registrations: <repo>/.git/worktrees/<env>/. The worktree directories and your work are untouched; only the registrations are deleted.

Rule: never run git worktree prune (or git worktree remove for another environment) inside a container. Run worktree maintenance on the host, where git can see every worktree.

Recovery. The worktree's own .git pointer file survives the prune, so the registration can be rewritten by hand. For each broken environment:

n=<env-name>                                   # e.g. my-project-my-feature
d=<main-repo>/.git/worktrees/$n
mkdir -p "$d"
echo "<worktree-root>/$n/.git"  > "$d/gitdir"     # bare path — no "gitdir: " prefix here
echo "../.."                    > "$d/commondir"
echo "ref: refs/heads/$n"       > "$d/HEAD"
(cd <worktree-root>/$n && git reset)   # rebuild the index from HEAD; working tree untouched

Then git worktree list on the host shows the environment again and the warning disappears. If the environment's branch is not named after the environment, put its real branch in HEAD.

If you would rather start over, ffleet remove SLUG and recreate — but check for unpushed work first.

docs.title: Environment shows as broken (workdir missing)
docs.text:
Symptom. An environment you created with ffleet up --here is listed with everything unknown and a workdir_missing warning:

$ ffleet ls
...
Warning: broken environment(s):
  - my-project-my-feature: workdir_missing
  Their work dir is gone; run `ffleet remove SLUG` to clear the stale record.

ffleet status my-feature shows the same broken: field and the directory the environment was registered for.

Cause. In-place environments run in a directory you chose, and Forge Fleet only records where it is. That directory was deleted or moved (or lives on a volume that is not mounted right now) — the environment's record outlived it.

Recovery. If the directory is only temporarily unavailable (an unmounted disk), mount it and the environment reports normally again — Forge Fleet never deletes a record on its own. Otherwise clear it:

$ ffleet remove my-feature

That stops any leftover container, deletes the environment's metadata and drops it from the in-place registry. Your files are not involved — the directory is already gone.

docs.title: Environment shows as broken (metadata missing)
docs.text:
Symptom. A directory sits in your worktree root under an environment's name, but Forge Fleet cannot read a session from it:

$ ffleet ls
...
Warning: broken environment(s):
  - my-project-my-feature: metadata_missing
  Their ffleet metadata is gone; run `ffleet remove SLUG` to clear them, then recreate with `ffleet up`.

Cause. The environment's session.json was deleted, truncated or otherwise made unreadable — most often by a git clean -fdx or git stash --all run inside a pre-#105 environment, which stored its metadata in the worktree itself. The worktree and your work are still there; only the record of the agent session is gone, so attach, tail and send no longer have a session to talk to.

Recovery. Check the worktree for work you want to keep (git -C <worktree-root>/<env> status), then clear and recreate:

$ ffleet remove my-feature
$ ffleet up my-feature

remove prompts before it acts and warns about uncommitted or unpushed work, so you see what is at stake first.

If remove refuses with "not registered as a worktree", the directory has also lost its git registration — recover that first, following worktree registration missing above, then run remove again.

docs.title: Environment shows as broken (worktree missing)
docs.text:
Symptom. A container is still listed — possibly running — but the worktree it was created for is gone:

$ ffleet ls
...
Warning: broken environment(s):
  - my-project-my-feature: worktree_missing
  Their worktree is gone while a container survives; run `ffleet remove SLUG` to stop and clear it.

Cause. The worktree directory was deleted outside Forge Fleet (rm -rf, a git worktree remove on the host, a wiped scratch disk). The container mounts that path, so the agent inside it is working on nothing; only the container and Forge Fleet's own record of the environment are left.

Recovery. There is nothing left to repair — the worktree held the work:

$ ffleet remove my-feature

That stops and removes the container and deletes the environment's metadata record. Any commits that only existed in the deleted worktree are gone with it; commits you had pushed are still on the remote, so ffleet up my-feature --from <branch> recreates a fresh environment on them.

docs.title: Container won't become ready in time
docs.text:
First-time image pulls or heavy setup can exceed the default readiness wait. Raise it:

$ ffleet up my-feature --wait-timeout 900

docs.title: Can't attach
docs.text:
• ffleet up SLUG attaches when the agent is live and relaunches it if not.
  • ffleet up SLUG --peek attaches only if it's already live and never relaunches — useful to check without side effects.
  • To detach cleanly once attached, use tmux Ctrl-B then D.

docs.title: Garbled characters or wrong colors after attaching
docs.text:
Attaching runs docker exec -it <env> tmux -u attach. docker exec hard-codes TERM=xterm and does not inherit your terminal, so Forge Fleet forwards the host's TERM, LANG, and COLORTERM into the exec — that keeps the tmux client matched to your real terminal instead of emitting mismatched escape sequences (stray/garbled characters). If your host TERM has no terminfo entry inside the container (common for kitty/ghostty/wezterm/foot), it is downgraded to xterm-256color so attach never fails with missing or unsuitable terminal. tmux -u forces UTF-8 rendering regardless of the container locale.

If you still see garbled output or missing colors with a custom image, make sure the image provides the same defaults the bundled one bakes in:

  • a UTF-8 locale (LANG, e.g. en_US.UTF-8),
  • a broad terminfo database (ncurses-term),
  • an /etc/tmux.conf with default-terminal tmux-256color, truecolor, and allow-passthrough on.

docs.title: When in doubt
docs.text:
• stop is safe and reversible; remove is not. Reach for stop first.
  • Your work lives in the worktree and the saved session, not the container — so rebuilding the container is cheap.
  • Still stuck? File an issue on ffleet-dist (see Feedback).

docs.title: How-to: completing & cleanup
docs.text:
When a piece of work is merged or abandoned, tear the environment down. When you're done with a whole project — or want to uninstall — clean up the ~/.forge-fleet registry. For full flags see the command reference.

flowchart TD
    E[Environment done] -->|ffleet remove SLUG| R[Worktree deleted; ffleet-created branch deleted]
    E -->|ffleet remove --done| S[Tick the landed ones; all removed in one pass]
    S --> D
    R --> D{More environments in this project?}
    D -->|yes| E
    D -->|no| P[Project-level cleanup]
    P -->|ffleet projects ls| L[See every known project and its environments]
    P -->|ffleet projects prune| PR[Drop stale entries + their ~/.forge-fleet home dirs]
    P -->|ffleet projects rm ID| RM[Delete one project's ~/.forge-fleet/ID dir + registry entry]

docs.title: Get your work out first
docs.text:
Forge Fleet manages environments, not your git workflow: it never pushes your branch or opens a PR for you. Landing the work is your job — or the agent's, from inside the container — and you must do it before remove, which deletes the branch Forge Fleet created.

Find the branch. A worktree environment lives on a branch named <project>-<slug> (the same name as its container). Confirm it with status:

$ ffleet status my-feature
...
branch: my-project-my-feature
worktree: ~/.forge-fleet/my-project/worktrees/my-feature

Push / open a PR — either ask the agent ("commit, push, and open a PR"), or do it yourself from the worktree:

$ ffleet goto my-feature
$ git push -u origin my-project-my-feature
$ gh pr create
$ exit

Push credentials are not provided by default. The container knows your origin URL but has no push auth — no SSH key, no gh/git token, no host git config. It does speak HTTPS to your remote's host (git_https_rewrite, on by default), so all you supply is a token: create a fine-grained personal access token scoped to this one repository and pass it through docker_env_file:

# docker.env
GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_…
GH_TOKEN=github_pat_…

Prefer that to mounting ~/.ssh: a mounted key is your real, long-lived credential, valid for every repository it can reach and for as long as the environment exists. Your commit identity (name/email) is forwarded automatically from [git] or your host git config — only push credentials need this. Prefer to stay fully local? git_local_main = true bases the branch on your local main so you can merge locally with no push at all.

Once credentials are in place, the agent can push on its own. If you want it to commit but never publish, set git_allow_origin_writes = false: it denies git push, gh pr create, gh pr merge, gh release create, gh workflow run and the common spellings of a mutating gh api call at the agent's own permission layer. Matching is by command prefix, so the coverage has edges worth reading before you rely on it — see the caveats. It pairs naturally with git_local_main but is independent of it — neither implies the other, so set both if you want a fully local-only environment.

Forge Fleet sandboxes your setup — it doesn't replace it. The real leverage is still your own prompts, your skills/subagents, and templates that wire an issue straight into a seeded session. Forge Fleet's job is to run all of that inside an isolated, disposable container — so you can let an agent work autonomously without it touching your host. It's the safe sandbox around your workflow, not a substitute for it.

docs.title: Remove one environment
docs.text:
ffleet remove SLUG tears the environment down: it stops the container and deletes the worktree. If Forge Fleet created the branch, that branch is deleted too; a branch you brought in with --from is left alone.

$ ffleet remove my-feature
$ ffleet remove my-feature -y   # skip the confirmation prompt

remove surfaces unpushed/uncommitted work before deleting so you don't lose it by surprise. This is irreversible — if you only want the container gone, use ffleet stop instead.

Before stopping the container, remove briefly asks the agent to exit on its own (/exit for Claude Code, /quit for Codex), waiting a few seconds at most. For Claude Code this is what makes it archive the session shown on claude.ai/code — otherwise you'd have to archive it by hand. stop deliberately skips this: a stopped environment is meant to come back, so its session is left active rather than archived.

Plain remove makes no network call at all: it is deliberately fast and offline-safe.

docs.title: See which environments have landed
docs.text:
ffleet ls has a PR column. For each environment it shows what the pull requests whose head branch is that environment's branch say about it:

PR shows What it means merged #4 the work landed merged #4,#7 it landed as a stack of pull requests open #9 still in review — nothing known: no pull request on that branch, only closed ones, or the lookup could not run

The match is on the branch, which is a first-class GitHub field — so it still works after the branch is deleted on merge. If the agent opened its pull request from a sub-branch instead of the environment's branch, the column reads —: the environment is shown, just never swept.

The lookup needs the gh CLI, and gh owns its own auth. Forge Fleet never handles a token, a key or any credential for this — run gh auth login once and that is the whole setup. gh is optional: with it missing, unauthenticated, or pointed at a repo with no origin, the column simply reads — and everything else works exactly as before — no error, no warning, same exit code. Projects on pm = "linear" or pm = "none" leave the column blank and never invoke gh at all.

docs.title: Sweep the landed environments (remove --done)
docs.text:
When several environments have finished, ffleet remove --done collapses N teardowns into one reviewed action:

$ ffleet remove --done
[forge-fleet] Refreshing remote refs (git fetch --prune)
Remove these landed environments:
  [x] fix-login   [my-project-fix-login]    merged #4
  [x] add-export  [my-project-add-export]   merged #7,#9
  [ ] flaky-test  [my-project-flaky-test]   merged #11  — unsaved work: uncommitted changes

Tick what you want gone and press enter. The checkmark is the approval — there is no second y/n prompt. Then a tally:

  fix-login: removed
  add-export: removed
  flaky-test: skipped (uncommitted changes)

removed 2, skipped 1, failed 0

Two independent things must both be true before an environment is offered:

  1. it landed — at least one merged pull request on its branch, and no open one;
  2. nothing would be lost — the same unsaved-work check plain remove runs.

A branch that is pushed but unreviewed is safe to delete yet not done; a merged branch with uncommitted changes is done yet not safe. An environment failing the second check is listed with its reason but never pre-ticked — you can still tick it deliberately. Every ambiguity resolves to "not swept": the worst case is that you clean up by hand, exactly as before.

Notes:

  • The sweep starts with one visible git fetch --prune, because the unsaved-work check reads your remote-tracking refs and is otherwise only as fresh as your last fetch. This is the only fetch in the teardown path; plain remove never fetches. A failed fetch is a warning, not a stop — the check just stays conservative.
  • A landed branch is not flagged just because its commits were squashed away: the check asks whether the default branch already contains the branch's content, not whether the commits themselves are there. Uncommitted changes and untracked files are still flagged on such a branch.
  • --done takes no SLUG. It sweeps, or it removes one — not both.
  • ffleet remove --done --yes skips the picker and removes every environment that is landed and clean. On a non-interactive stdin (CI, a pipe) --yes is required — without it the command errors rather than acting silently.
  • Nothing is ever removed unattended: there is no auto-removal on any trigger.

docs.title: The project registry (~/.forge-fleet)
docs.text:
Forge Fleet tracks the projects it knows about in ~/.forge-fleet/registry.json, with each project's home data under ~/.forge-fleet/{id}/. The ffleet projects commands manage that registry — useful for multi-project cleanup and uninstalling.

  • ffleet projects ls — every known project with its environments grouped under it (add --json). Start here: each header carries the project's registry id, which is what projects rm takes. Bare ffleet projects does the same.
$ ffleet projects ls
project: my-project  [my-project-1a2b3c4d]  /repos/my-project
  • ffleet projects prune — remove stale registry entries and delete their ~/.forge-fleet home directories. Good housekeeping after you've deleted repos. Prompts first; -y to skip.
$ ffleet projects prune
  • ffleet projects rm PROJECT_ID — permanently delete one project's ~/.forge-fleet/{id} directory and its registry entry. Prompts first; -y to skip.
$ ffleet projects rm my-project-1a2b3c4d

docs.title: Uninstalling Forge Fleet
docs.text:
To leave no trace:

  1. ffleet remove every remaining environment (or ffleet ls per project to find them).
  2. ffleet projects prune, or ffleet projects rm ID for each project, to clear ~/.forge-fleet.
  3. Delete the ffleet binary from your PATH.

Removing environments deletes worktrees and ffleet-created branches — double-check nothing is unpushed first.

docs.title: How-to: starting an environment
docs.text:
Everything happens through ffleet up SLUG. This page covers the choices you make when creating an environment. For the exhaustive flag list see the command reference; for the equivalent ffleet.toml keys see the config reference.

flowchart TD
    A[ffleet up SLUG] --> B{git-mode?}
    B -->|auto / worktree / clone| C[new isolated worktree + branch]
    B -->|off, or --here| D[in-place: your current directory, no worktree]
    C --> E{seed a prompt?}
    D --> E
    E -->|-p / --prompt| F[fresh agent session, seeded]
    E -->|--prompt-file FILE| F
    E -->|no prompt| G[fresh agent session, empty]
    F --> H{attach?}
    G --> H
    H -->|default, or --attach| I[attached — steer the agent live]
    H -->|--no-attach, -y, or attach = false| J[running in the background]
    H -->|--peek| K[attach only if already live; never launch]

docs.title: Seeding the work: prompts
docs.text:
• -p / --prompt "…" — the initial message for a fresh session. On an existing/revived session the prompt is instead sent to the live agent.
  • --prompt-file PATH — read the prompt from a file (handy for long or multi-line instructions) instead of --prompt.
$ ffleet up my-feature -p "Refactor the auth module and add tests"
$ ffleet up my-feature --prompt-file ./task.md

docs.title: Attach behaviour
docs.text:
• Default: after starting, you're attached to the agent's tmux session.
  • --no-attach — start (or revive) but stay in your shell; good for background runs. Check in later with status / tail, or attach with a plain ffleet up.
  • --attach — attach explicitly. Only needed to override a project that defaults to not attaching (below), or a -y run; passing both flags is an error.
  • -y / --yes — unattended mode never attaches unless you pass --attach (or use --peek, which always attaches when the agent is live), so a scripted or CI run can't hang on an interactive session. It overrides attach = true and ATTACH=true too.
  • attach = false in ffleet.toml — make not attaching this project's default, for a repo you normally drive in the background. Either flag still wins per run, as does an ATTACH env var. See the config reference.
  • --peek — a strict, side-effect-free peek: attach only if the agent is already live, and never relaunch it. Use it to look without risk of starting anything.
  • --wait-timeout N — seconds to wait for the container/agent to become ready (default 300). Raise it for heavy first-time image pulls or slow setup.

docs.title: In-place mode: --here (works without git)
docs.text:
--here starts (or revives) an agent over your current directory — no worktree, no branch. This is the "not only programming / works without git" case: point an agent at any folder.

$ cd ~/notes
$ ffleet up braindump --here -p "Organise these notes into a coherent outline"

Because there's no worktree isolation, the agent works directly in that directory. It's still a registered environment (shows in ls, revivable with up), and remove cleans up its metadata without touching your directory. It's the no-worktree, no-git case — closely related to running with --git-mode off.

Setting git_mode = "off" in ffleet.toml makes this the default for the project: ffleet up SLUG then runs in-place over the project root (from any subdirectory) with no worktree and no git repo required — you don't need to pass --here each time. This is the way to run Forge Fleet on a plain, non-git folder.

docs.title: Choosing the coding assistant
docs.text:
• --coding-agent claude|codex — which assistant to launch (default claude). The project default comes from default in ffleet.toml.
  • Per-agent config lives in the [claude] and [codex] tables of ffleet.toml: the credential/config directory (dir), the credential auth source, the binary (cmd), the default model and reasoning effort, and your own extra_args. See controlling the coding assistant.
$ ffleet up my-feature --coding-agent codex -p "…"

The chosen agent is fixed at create time — switching agents means a new environment.

docs.title: Selecting a subagent
docs.text:
• --subagent NAME — launch a specific custom agent (e.g. code-reviewer). Works with or without -t/--template: it no longer requires a template just to pick a subagent. If the template also configures a subagent, --subagent wins and a warning is printed when the two differ. See templates for the template-config equivalent.
$ ffleet up my-feature --coding-agent claude --subagent code-reviewer -p "…"

Like --coding-agent, the subagent is fixed at create time (reviving an existing environment always ignores --subagent).

Support differs by coding-agent:

  • Claude — deterministic. Translated straight into Claude Code's own --agent <name> flag, so the CLI itself enforces the agent exists and is used.
  • Codex — best-effort. The Codex CLI has no equivalent flag, so ffleet looks up NAME in ~/.codex/agents/*.toml (personal) or .codex/agents/*.toml in the repo (project) — matched on the file's name field, not the filename — and, once found, weaves a delegation instruction into the launch prompt (or sends it into the pane on an interactive launch with no prompt) asking Codex to use it. Codex decides for itself whether to follow that instruction — nothing in ffleet forces it, so treat it as a strong hint, not a guarantee.

docs.title: Git modes
docs.text:
--git-mode auto|worktree|clone|off (default auto) decides how git is set up inside the container:

  • worktree — a git worktree on a new branch off the source repo (the isolated default; auto resolves to this in a normal repo).
  • clone — reserved for a fresh clone instead of a worktree; not implemented yet, so an environment configured with it fails to start.
  • off — no git integration; the agent works directly in the mounted directory (the same "works without git" case as --here). Set as git_mode = "off" in ffleet.toml, plain ffleet up SLUG runs in-place over the project root — no worktree, no git repo, and no --here needed.
  • auto — pick the sensible mode for the repo.

Full walkthrough, plus commit identity and denying the agent remote writes: git options.

docs.title: Basing a worktree on an existing branch
docs.text:
• --from BRANCH — base a first-time worktree on an existing branch instead of a new empty one (ignored once the environment exists).
  • --git-local-main — base the worktree on your local main and keep completion local-only (no push/PR). Pairs with git_local_main in config.
$ ffleet up hotfix --from release-2.3 -p "Cherry-pick the logging fix"

New to git worktrees? They let multiple branches be checked out at once in separate directories — see Git's own git worktree documentation.

docs.title: Where worktrees are created
docs.text:
worktree_root controls where per-environment worktrees live. ffleet init proposes a default that follows the config location you chose:

  • Home mode (default) — a folder under ~/.forge-fleet/{project-id}/worktrees, keeping the setup fully local to your machine with nothing to commit into a shared project.
  • Local mode — .forge-fleet/worktrees inside the checkout, so config and state stay next to the repo (that directory is already added to .gitignore).

worktree_root is set once by ffleet init (it accepts --worktree-root to seed the value) and thereafter read straight from ffleet.toml. To change it, edit the config — there is no per-run override on the env commands.

docs.title: Templates (brief)
docs.text:
-t / --template <id> seeds a fresh environment from a [templates.<id>] table in ffleet.toml — typically fetching an issue from your PM tool and rendering a prompt from it. In template mode the SLUG argument is the template ref (e.g. an issue number):

$ ffleet up -t task 123

Full guide, including PM-tool integration (GitHub Issues, Linear): templates.md.

docs.title: Docker-related start options (brief)
docs.text: Several flags shape the container: --image, --extra-mounts, --extra-hosts, --docker-env-file, --docker-host-bind, --uv-cache-dir, plus the credential dirs --claude-dir / --codex-dir / --claude-auth. They're summarized in the command reference; the full explanations are in container-config.md, secrets.md, and docker-dood.md.

docs.title: How-to: working with a running environment
docs.text:
Your environment is up. This page is about living with it day to day — attaching, detaching, inspecting, and parking it without losing work. For full flag detail see the command reference.

flowchart TD
    R[Running environment] -->|ffleet up SLUG| A[Attached to agent session]
    A -->|detach: Ctrl-B D| R
    R -->|ffleet goto SLUG| S[Shell in the worktree]
    S -->|exit| R
    R -->|ffleet ls / status / tail / path| I[Inspect: no state change]
    R -->|ffleet stop SLUG| P[Stopped: container gone, worktree+branch+metadata kept]
    P -->|ffleet up SLUG| A

docs.title: Selecting an environment
docs.text:
Every environment command (up, remove, goto, stop, tail, status, path, continue) takes an optional SLUG. Omit it and Forge Fleet first tries to resolve the environment from your current directory; if that doesn't match, it opens an interactive picker:

  • On a capable terminal you get an arrow-key highlight bar — move with ↑/↓ and press Enter to choose. For ffleet up, the list ends with a "create a new environment" entry.
  • On a plain terminal (TERM=dumb, NO_COLOR, or no ANSI support) it degrades to a numbered 1) 2) 3) menu — type a number and press Enter.

When stdin isn't a terminal (a pipe or CI), no picker is shown: pass SLUG explicitly, or you'll get a "SLUG is required…" error.

docs.title: Attach & detach
docs.text:
• Attach: ffleet up SLUG drops you into the agent's session (when it's live). That's the same command you used to start it.
  • Detach: press tmux's Ctrl-B then D. This leaves the agent running — you're just stepping out. Re-attach later with ffleet up SLUG.
  • Peek without risk: ffleet up SLUG --peek attaches only if the agent is already live and never relaunches anything.

docs.title: goto — a shell in the worktree (not the agent)
docs.text:
ffleet goto SLUG opens a shell in the environment's worktree directory — distinct from attaching to the agent. Use it to inspect files, run a command, or make a manual edit alongside the agent. Leave it with exit.

$ ffleet goto my-feature   # you're now in the worktree
$ git log --oneline -5
$ exit

Related: ffleet path SLUG just prints the worktree path, so you can cd "$(ffleet path my-feature)" from your own shell.

docs.title: Environment metadata — where it lives
docs.text:
Each environment has a small metadata directory (session.json, container.git, claude.json) recording its live state — which container it maps to, the agent session to resume, and git bookkeeping. Forge Fleet reads it for ffleet ls / status and to resume your session on the next up.

New environments keep this outside the checkout, under ~/.forge-fleet/{project-id}/worktree-meta/{env-name}/. This keeps it outside the reach of even aggressive in-worktree cleanup — git clean -fdx, git stash --all — which can't delete it or orphan the container. You never need to tiptoe around a .forge-fleet/ directory in your worktree.

Older environments (created before this change) still keep the directory in-worktree at <worktree>/.forge-fleet/. There's no migration — they keep working. For those, deleting the directory by hand still orphans the environment, so use ffleet stop / ffleet remove to tear one down rather than removing files. Forge Fleet marks that in-worktree directory as ignored (via the worktree's info/exclude) so routine git stash -u / git clean -fd won't touch it, but git clean -fdx / git stash --all / rm -rf .forge-fleet still would.

Either way: to tear an environment down, use ffleet stop or ffleet remove — never delete metadata by hand.

docs.title: Inspecting
docs.text:
None of these change state:

  • ffleet ls — all environments for the project (add --json for scripts). ffleet projects ls widens that to every registered project.
  • ffleet status SLUG — live status: container up?, agent live/exited, what the agent is doing and why we say so (add --json for scripts).
  • ffleet tail SLUG — the last lines of the agent's transcript (-n/--lines N, default 100).
  • ffleet path SLUG — the worktree/working-directory path.

docs.title: Is the agent still working?
docs.text:
Forge Fleet answers that from what the environment can actually show: whether the container is up, whether the agent's terminal pane is still alive, and the agent's own session transcript — the record each agent writes as it works. It reports one of four states in the AGENT_STATE column:

State Meaning working mid-turn: thinking, or running a tool. idle it finished its turn; the next move is yours. exited the agent process is gone (the container may still be up). unknown there is no evidence to read — see the probe reason in status. 
$ ffleet ls
project: my-project
SHORT        ENV                     AGENT   CONTAINER               CONTAINER_STATE  RUNTIME  LAST_ACTIVITY              AGENT_STATE
-----------  ----------------------  ------  ----------------------  ---------------  -------  -------------------------  -----------
add-logging  my-project-add-logging  claude  my-project-add-logging  running          running  2026-08-12T09:14:22+00:00  working
fix-auth     my-project-fix-auth     claude  my-project-fix-auth     running          running  2026-08-12T09:12:03+00:00  idle

LAST_ACTIVITY is when the agent last did something (its last transcript record), not when Forge Fleet last touched the environment.

The RUNTIME column is the layer below: whether the container is up (stopped, starting, running, failed, unknown). starting means the container is up and the agent is still coming up — normally a few seconds. An environment that is still without an agent two minutes after its container started reads as failed instead: the agent never came up, or died at launch. Relaunch it with ffleet up SLUG (see Troubleshooting).

status adds the why: the probe reason behind the state, and the raw evidence it was derived from.

$ ffleet status add-logging
Environment status
  name: my-project-add-logging
  slug: add-logging
  branch: my-project-add-logging
  agent: claude
  runtime: running
  agent state: working
  probe reason: tool call pending
  last activity: 2026-08-12T09:14:22+00:00
  evidence: liveness=running, pane=alive, source=transcript, pending_tool=Bash
  container: my-project-add-logging
  session id: 6f1c…
  tmux session: main
  worktree: ~/.forge-fleet/my-project/worktrees/add-logging

Two things worth knowing:

  • Both agents report real state. Claude Code is read from its per-session transcript, Codex from the session rollout it writes under --codex-dir (~/.codex/sessions/…), matched to the environment by the working directory it was started in.
  • unknown is never an error by itself. It says the evidence was missing — a fresh environment whose agent has not written anything yet, a stopped container, or a session whose transcript is gone. For Codex that also covers an environment created by an older Forge Fleet, whose container works from /workspace instead of the worktree path the rollout records. Runtime state, attach and tail all work as usual either way.

For scripts, ffleet ls --json carries agent_state plus the raw probe_reason token (turn_ended, tool_call_pending, agent_thinking, agent_exited, runtime_not_running, runtime_starting, tmux_session_missing, transcript_absent, transcript_unreadable, adapter_not_supported), alongside runtime_state.

It also carries broken_reason — empty for a healthy environment, and otherwise one of:

  • worktree_registration_missing — the environment's git registration was deleted (recovery)
  • workdir_missing — an in-place environment whose working directory is gone (recovery)
  • metadata_missing — a worktree directory whose session.json is gone or unreadable (recovery)
  • worktree_missing — a surviving container whose worktree was deleted (recovery)

The table prints the same information as a warning under the rows. Broken environments are listed so you can see and clear them: ffleet remove SLUG tears each one down, while restore and remove --done skip them.

Changed in this release. Agent state used to be inferred by diffing the terminal 400 ms apart, and an unchanging screen was reported as waiting for input. That guess is gone, along with the BLOCKED_REASON column and the blocked_reason JSON field — read agent_state / probe_reason instead.

docs.title: stop — park it without losing work
docs.text:
ffleet stop SLUG removes the container but keeps the worktree, branch, and metadata. It's the safe "get this out of the way" move — reversible, unlike remove.

$ ffleet stop my-feature   # container gone, everything else preserved
$ ffleet up   my-feature   # revive: rebuilt from config, session resumed, no data loss

Because containers run with --rm, there's no lingering "stopped container" — a stop removes it, and up rebuilds a fresh one when you come back. Your work lives in the worktree and the saved session, not the container.

ffleet projects stop does the same for every environment on the machine — the whole fleet parked in one command. Each one is recorded as parked, so a later ffleet projects restore leaves them down; ffleet up SLUG brings one back.

For Claude agents, session resume is exact — it reattaches this environment's own last session. For Codex agents it's best-effort: Codex resumes the most recently used session (filtered to sessions started from the same working directory) rather than one by ID. Since each environment's container workspace is mounted at its own host-identical path, this resolves correctly for concurrent environments in the common case even though they share --codex-dir by default — see the container-config note for the mechanism and the fallback if you ever hit a mismatch.

docs.title: restore — bring everything back after a reboot
docs.text:
A host restart — or restarting the Docker daemon — takes every container with it. Your worktrees, branches and saved sessions are untouched, but the agents are gone. ffleet restore brings back, in one go, every environment that was supposed to be running:

$ ffleet restore           # this project
$ ffleet projects restore  # every project you've run `ffleet init` in
project my-app
  my-feature: restored
  spike: skipped (parked)
  review: skipped (already running)

restored 1, skipped 2, failed 0
  • It respects what you asked for. Only environments whose last recorded intent was "running" come back. Anything you parked with ffleet stop stays parked. Environments that predate this feature have no recorded intent at all, so they are left alone too — restore never guesses. Your first restore after upgrading may therefore do nothing; one ffleet up (or ffleet stop) per environment records the intent, and restore picks it up from then on.
  • It brings back containers, not dead agents. Restore is for the case where the containers are gone. An environment whose container is still up is reported "already running" and left as-is, even if the agent inside it exited — use ffleet up SLUG for that one.
  • Nothing is sent, nothing is attached. The agents come back idle, exactly where they left off; attach with ffleet up SLUG when you want one.
  • Safe to re-run. An environment that is already up is reported as such and left alone.
  • One failure doesn't stop the rest. Each environment is reported on its own line; the command exits non-zero if any of them failed.

ffleet projects restore works from any directory — it walks the projects you've registered with ffleet init, so you don't have to visit each repo. A project you never ran ffleet init in has nothing recorded to restore.

docs.title: Working inside tmux
docs.text:
When you attach, you're inside a tmux session running the agent. You mostly just type at the agent, but a few tmux things are worth knowing:

  • Detach: Ctrl-B then D — leaves the agent running. The one key you must know.
  • Scroll back: the mouse wheel may not reach the agent's history. Enter copy-mode with Ctrl-B then [, scroll with arrows/PageUp, q to exit.
  • Copy / paste: tmux captures mouse selection, so a normal drag-select may not hit your clipboard. Hold Shift while selecting to use your terminal's own copy/paste (works in most terminals). Or copy within tmux via copy-mode (Ctrl-B [, select, Enter) and paste that buffer with Ctrl-B ].

New to tmux? See the tmux wiki or a shortcut cheat sheet.

Kept deliberately simple: one tmux session per container, a single pane (0). You can split extra panes yourself, but multiple tmux sessions — and attaching from inside another tmux (tmux-in-tmux) — are not supported.

docs.title: Beyond tmux: driving Claude Code from the web
docs.text:
Attaching over tmux is Forge Fleet's built-in way to reach the agent, and it works for any agent. But if the agent is Claude Code, Claude Code can also expose its own session to the web — so you can watch and steer it from a browser or phone without ffleet up or tmux at all:

  • Remote Control — continue this session from another device via claude.ai/code. Execution stays inside the Forge Fleet container; you just reconnect to it from the web. This is the natural fit for detached/background work — start it here, keep an eye on it from anywhere.
  • Claude Code on the web — the fully hosted cousin, where sessions run on Anthropic-managed infra. Mentioned for completeness; it's a different execution model than Forge Fleet's containers.

Remote Control is a Claude Code feature, configured inside the agent (not by Forge Fleet), and has no equivalent for other agents such as Codex. Forge Fleet's tmux attach/detach above keeps working regardless.

Forge Fleet does name each Claude session after its environment (<project>-<slug>) and gives the container a matching hostname, so entries in Remote Control and the /resume picker are identifiable at a glance.

docs.title: What can and can't change mid-life
docs.text:
When ffleet up rebuilds a stopped/broken environment, it refreshes config-derived settings from your current ffleet.toml/flags and saves them back. But identity/continuity settings are fixed at create time — to change those you must remove and recreate.

Refreshed on the next up (revive-time-mutable) Fixed at create (need remove to change) image branch extra_mounts worktree extra_hosts in-place vs worktree mode docker_env_file git-mode credential auth coding agent credential dirs (~/.claude / ~/.codex) the session agent cmd / extra_args agent model / reasoning effort

So: to pick up a new image, an added mount, or a changed env file, just ffleet stop then ffleet up. To change the branch, git-mode, or which agent runs, ffleet remove and start fresh. This is the practical face of config precedence.

docs.title: ffleet
docs.text:
Forge Fleet — spin up isolated, containerized coding-agent environments.

Usage:
  ffleet [command]

Available Commands:
  completion  Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
  goto        Open a shell in an environment's worktree. Leave it with `exit`.
  help        Help about any command
  init        Set up ffleet.toml for the current project (home-based by default, specs/017).
  ls          List all environments for the project (add --json for machine-readable output).
  path        Print the worktree/working directory path for an environment (for cd "$(ffleet path)").
  projects    Act on every registered project: the whole-machine view and the machine-wide verbs.
  remove      Tear down an environment: stop the container, delete the worktree and (if ffleet created it) the branch.
  restore     Bring back every environment that should be running (after a host or Docker restart).
  status      Show the live status of an environment (container, runtime and agent state).
  stop        Stop an environment's container, keeping the worktree, branch and metadata.
  tail        Print the last lines of an agent's transcript for an environment.
  up          Start or resume an environment. State — not flags — decides what happens.
  version     Print the ffleet version and build metadata

Flags:
  -h, --help      help for ffleet
  -v, --version   version for ffleet

Use "ffleet [command] --help" for more information about a command.

docs.title: ffleet up
docs.text:
Start or resume an environment. State — not flags — decides what happens.

Absent env -> create it; a live session -> attach; a stopped container or dead
agent -> rebuild from the current config and resume. On that rebuild, config-
derived settings (image, mounts, hosts, env-file, auth, dirs, agent cmd/model/reasoning/args)
refresh from the current config and are saved back; identity/continuity settings
(branch, worktree, mode, git-mode, agent, session) stay fixed at create.

Your shell's directory is never changed — use 'ffleet goto' to enter a worktree.

Usage:
  ffleet up [SLUG] [flags]

Flags:
      --attach                   Attach to the agent session afterwards, overriding the 'attach' config key.
      --claude-auth string       Claude credential source: auto, keychain, token, api-key, credentials-file, or external. (default "auto")
      --claude-dir string        Host ~/.claude dir to mount for credentials/config. (default "~/.claude")
      --codex-dir string         Host ~/.codex dir to mount for credentials/config. (default "~/.codex")
      --coding-agent string      Coding assistant to launch inside the container (e.g. claude, codex). (default "claude")
      --copy-files string        Gitignored files to snapshot from the main repo into a new worktree, comma-separated relative paths.
      --docker-env-file string   Env file passed to the container (docker --env-file).
      --docker-host-bind         Mount the host Docker socket so the agent can drive the host's Docker daemon (Docker-outside-of-Docker).
      --extra-hosts string       Extra host mappings passed to docker --add-host, comma-separated 'host:address'.
      --extra-mounts string      Additional docker mounts, comma-separated 'host:container[:ro|:rw]'.
      --from string              Base a first-time worktree on an existing branch (ignored once the env exists).
      --git-local-main           Base the worktree on the local main branch instead of the remote.
      --git-mode string          How git is set up in the container: auto, worktree, clone, or off. (default "auto")
  -h, --help                     help for up
      --here                     In-place mode: start/revive an agent over the current directory (no worktree).
      --image string             Docker image to run the agent in. (default "ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-python:latest")
      --no-attach                Do not attach to the agent session afterwards, overriding the 'attach' config key.
      --peek                     Strict, side-effect-free peek: attach only if the agent is live, never relaunch.
  -p, --prompt string            Message: seeds a fresh session, otherwise sent to the live/revived one.
      --prompt-file string       Read the prompt from a file instead of --prompt.
      --subagent string          Custom agent to launch (e.g. code-reviewer): a deterministic --agent flag on Claude, a best-effort delegation instruction on Codex (create-only; see docs). Overrides a template's configured subagent.
  -t, --template string          Seed a fresh env from a templates.<id> table in ffleet.toml; SLUG is the template ref.
      --uv-cache-dir string      Host uv cache dir to mount for faster installs. (default "~/.cache/uv")
      --wait-timeout int         Seconds to wait for the container/agent to become ready. (default 300)
  -y, --yes                      Unattended: skip the image-freshness pull prompt (warn only, never pull) and do not attach unless --attach is given.

docs.title: ffleet remove
docs.text:
Tear down an environment: stop the container, delete the worktree and
(if ffleet created it) the branch.

With --done it sweeps instead of removing one: it refreshes the remote refs,
then offers a multiselect of every environment whose branch has a merged pull
request and no open one. Ticking an entry is the approval — there is no second
prompt. An environment with unsaved work is listed with its reason but never
pre-ticked. The pull-request lookup needs the 'gh' CLI and a 'pm = "github"'
project; without either, nothing is offered and plain 'remove' still works.

Usage:
  ffleet remove [SLUG] [flags]

Aliases:
  remove, rm

Flags:
      --done   Sweep landed environments: pick from the ones whose pull request merged and remove them in one pass.
  -h, --help   help for remove
  -y, --yes    Skip the confirmation prompt.

docs.title: Config reference (ffleet.toml)
docs.text:
Every ffleet.toml setting. This file is a per-project, personal dev-tool preference — not team config. ffleet init writes it by default under ~/.forge-fleet/{project-id}/ffleet.toml ("home mode"), so nothing needs to be committed into the repo it configures. In-repo ("local mode") is supported as an explicit opt-in.

Most CLI flags mirror a key here; where they overlap the flag wins for that run (see config precedence). The canonical, fully-commented template is ffleet.toml.example at the repo root.

docs.title: What init sets, and everything else
docs.text:
ffleet init runs a short wizard for the settings most worth choosing up front — the default coding agent, the base image (python or go variant), the git mode, and whether sandboxes get host Docker access (DooD). Each question is pre-selected at its default, so pressing enter through them keeps today's behavior; your choices are written as active keys. Every other setting is written commented-out at its default, so the generated file doubles as a menu — uncomment and edit what you need.

init -y accepts every default without prompting. Non-default values for any other setting are configured by editing the generated ffleet.toml.

init is create-only: it never overwrites an existing config. To change settings later, edit the ffleet.toml directly — init prints its path when it writes it, and re-running init on a configured project just points you back at that file.

docs.title: Global keys
docs.text: Key Type Default Meaning project_name string — (required) Logical project name; used to name containers and worktrees. source_dir string — Absolute path to the source repo. Required in home mode; in local mode it's derived from where this file lives (set it only if the file isn't colocated with the repo). worktree_root string — (required) Where per-environment worktrees are created (absolute, or relative to the repo root). Inside the checkout (e.g. .forge-fleet/worktrees) or a separate folder under $HOME. image string ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-python:latest Docker image the agent container runs. Use ghcr.io/grzegorz-aniol/forge-fleet-go:latest for the Go-dev variant. git_mode string auto Git integration: auto | off | worktree | clone. off needs no git repo — ffleet up then runs in-place over the project root (no worktree, no --here). clone is reserved and not implemented yet. See git options. git_local_main bool false Base the worktree on the local main branch and keep completion local-only (no push/PR). See git options. attach bool true Whether ffleet up attaches to the agent session after starting it. Set false for a project you normally drive in the background; --attach / --no-attach override it per run, and ffleet up -y never attaches unless --attach is given. docker_host_bind bool false Let the agent inside the container drive the host Docker daemon (binds the host docker socket; agent-started containers become siblings). See DooD. git_allow_origin_writes bool true When false, deny the agent the outward-facing commands (git push, gh pr create, gh pr merge, gh release create, gh workflow run, and gh api with a mutating method right after api). Sticky per environment. See denying remote writes. git_https_rewrite bool true Rewrite git remotes to HTTPS inside the container (url."https://<host>/".insteadOf "git@<host>:"), so the agent needs no SSH key. Written into the container's own gitconfig only — never the repository's. See HTTPS remotes in the container. uv_cache_dir string ~/.cache/uv Shared uv cache mounted into the container for faster installs. extra_mounts list — Extra bind mounts as source:target[:ro\|:rw]. Target must be an absolute container path; a relative source resolves against the repo root; ~ expands to the host home. An optional :ro/:rw suffix sets the mode (default read-write). extra_hosts list — (may be omitted) Host-to-address mappings passed to docker run --add-host, each host:address. host-gateway resolves to the host itself. docker_env_file string — Additional env file passed to docker run --env-file (runtime secrets/keys). A relative path resolves against this config file's own directory. copy_files list — Gitignored files to snapshot from the main repo into each new worktree (globs allowed), so e.g. .env appears at the same relative path inside. One-time copy at creation, not a live link. default string — Which coding-agent ffleet up runs when none is named on the CLI. Must be one of the [section] names below (e.g. claude, codex). pm string github Issue tracker for -t templates: github (via gh CLI) | linear (needs LINEAR_API_KEY) | none (don't fetch; raw ref exposed as {id}). On any fetch failure ffleet warns and continues as pm=none. Also gates the PR column in ls and the remove --done sweep: only github consults the forge; linear/none leave the column blank and never invoke gh. check_image_period_days int or "off" 30 How often ffleet up checks whether a newer image exists in the registry (see image freshness check). Any positive integer sets the period in days; "off" disables the check entirely.

docs.title: Image freshness check (check_image_period_days)
docs.text:
Whenever ffleet up actually builds or (re)starts a container, and at least check_image_period_days have elapsed since the last check for this project, it does a best-effort comparison of the configured image against its remote counterpart. It compares two registry manifests: the one the tag resolves to right now, and the one behind the digest the local copy was pulled under. They differ only when the tag has actually moved, so the answer doesn't depend on which image store (classic or containerd) your Docker daemon uses:

  • Interactive session — if a newer image is found, ffleet prompts before pulling and pulls only on explicit approval, then starts the container from the freshly pulled image. The pull reports Docker's own outcome, so you can see whether anything was downloaded or the local copy was already current.
  • ffleet up -y / --yes — warn-only: ffleet prints a notice that a newer image exists but never prompts and never pulls. Pull it yourself with docker pull <image> (or run ffleet up interactively).

The check never blocks or fails ffleet up: if the registry is unreachable, or the image was built locally and so has no registry digest to compare, ffleet silently skips the comparison and starts the container as usual. The last-check timestamp is stored per project in ~/.forge-fleet/registry.json (not in ffleet.toml), so a project that was never checked is treated as due on its next up. Set check_image_period_days = "off" to disable the whole flow.

docs.title: [git] — identity injected into the container
docs.text:
Both keys must be set together — setting exactly one is an error. With neither, identity resolves from the environment's recorded value or your host git config; see commit identity.

Key Type Meaning user_name string Git author/committer name inside the container. user_email string Git author/committer email inside the container.

docs.title: [claude] / [codex] — per-coding-agent config
docs.text: Key Type Default Meaning dir string ~/.claude / ~/.codex Host directory mounted as the agent's config/credentials, so it's authenticated inside the container. auth string auto (Claude) Credential source ffleet injects. See the table below. cmd string the section name Override the binary invoked in the container (e.g. claude). model string the agent's own default Model the agent launches with, passed as --model <value>. Opaque — ffleet hands it to the binary unchecked. reasoning string the agent's own default Reasoning effort. On Claude, passed as --effort <value> (low, medium, high, xhigh, max). On Codex, which has no flag of its own for it, injected as -c model_reasoning_effort=<value>. extra_args list — Your own arguments for the agent, placed immediately after the binary (after model / reasoning when set) and before ffleet's own flags (e.g. ["--agent", "myagent"]). See controlling the coding assistant. extend_system_prompt bool true (Claude) Let ffleet append short, factual notes about the environment to the agent's system prompt. See below.

docs.title: git_allow_origin_writes
docs.text:
Agents run inside the container with their own approval prompts disabled, so once the container has push credentials nothing but the agent's judgement stops it from publishing work you have not reviewed. Setting git_allow_origin_writes = false mounts two small, ffleet-generated policy files read-only into the container — /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json and /etc/codex/requirements.toml — which deny these command prefixes at the agent's own permission layer:

git push · gh pr create · gh pr merge · gh release create · gh workflow run · gh api with a mutating method (POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE)

Each method is denied in the five spellings gh accepts immediately after gh api: --method POST, --method=POST, -X POST, -X=POST and -XPOST.

The agent can still commit locally; it just cannot publish. With extend_system_prompt on, Claude is also told why the commands fail, so a refusal reads as a known constraint rather than a mystery.

Caveats worth knowing:

  • Both agents match by command prefix, so a command wrapped in another shell (sh -c "git push") is not caught. This layer raises the bar; it is not a sandbox.
  • A gh api method flag placed after the resource path is not caught either — gh api repos/o/r/issues --method POST slips through, for the same prefix-matching reason. Nor are lowercase method tokens (--method post).
  • It is independent of git_local_main — neither implies the other. They pair naturally (a local-only base branch plus no way to publish), so set both if that is what you want.

Nothing is mounted for a brand-new environment when the key is absent or true, which is the default: remote writes are allowed unless you opt out.

The setting is sticky per environment. Once an environment has been created or started with a value, a later start with the key absent from your config keeps the persisted value rather than resetting it to the default — dropping git_allow_origin_writes = false from ffleet.toml does not quietly re-open remote writes. To re-enable them for an existing environment, set git_allow_origin_writes = true explicitly; an explicit value always wins.

docs.title: git_https_rewrite
docs.text:
Agent containers get no SSH key. To keep git fetch/git push working for a checkout whose origin is an SSH URL, the container's init script writes a rewrite into its own /home/buddy/.gitconfig at every start:

[url "https://github.com/"]
    insteadOf = git@github.com:
    insteadOf = ssh://git@github.com/

The host is derived from the checkout's origin URL, so a GitLab or Bitbucket remote gets its own host. The repository's git config is never touched — it is shared with the host and every other environment, so the container's transport choice must not leak into it.

The rewrite only changes how the container reaches the remote; it mints no credential. Supply one yourself as a repo-scoped fine-grained token through docker_env_file — see secrets.

Set git_https_rewrite = false to turn the rewrite off (for example when you deliberately mount your own SSH agent socket). Unlike git_allow_origin_writes it is not persisted per environment: every start re-reads it from your config.

docs.title: [claude].extend_system_prompt
docs.text:
With this on (the default), ffleet tells Claude a few facts about the environment it is running in, so it doesn't have to guess. Today there are two: when docker_host_bind is enabled, Claude is told that Docker runs in docker-outside-of-docker mode and that containers it starts are siblings of its own container — see Docker outside Docker; and when git_allow_origin_writes is false, Claude is told which outward-facing commands are denied and why. Nothing is added when both are at their defaults, and the key has no effect on Codex.

The notes are merged with any --append-system-prompt you set in extra_args, never replacing it: both end up in a single flag, with ffleet's text first and yours last. They are recomputed at every launch and are not stored in the environment's session.json. Set extend_system_prompt = false to opt out entirely — the launch command is then exactly what you configured.

docs.title: [claude].auth values
docs.text:
Value Behaviour auto Try keychain, then token, then api-key, then credentials-file; first available wins (default). keychain macOS only; pin the Keychain-derived credential (fails fast if the lookup fails). token Pin CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (from claude setup-token). api-key Pin ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (API billing, not subscription). credentials-file Pin the ~/.claude mount's .credentials.json (Linux only). external Skip the auth preflight entirely — you provide credentials another way (e.g. docker_env_file).

See container configuration for how these mounts and credentials fit together.

docs.title: [templates.<id>] — prompt templates
docs.text:
Looked up by ffleet up -t <id> <ref>: ffleet fetches issue <ref> from the configured pm source, derives the slug from the issue title, and renders prompt_template with the issue's fields.

Key Type Meaning prompt_template string Template rendered with {number}, {title}, {body}, {url}, {id} (raw ref), plus any extra key=value tokens passed on the CLI. subagent string Optional subagent for envs seeded from this template. On Claude, translated to a deterministic --agent <name> flag. On Codex, a best-effort delegation instruction woven into the launch prompt (or sent into the pane on an interactive launch) — Codex has no equivalent CLI flag, so this is not guaranteed; see starting. Using it with any other coding-agent errors. The up --subagent NAME flag is the per-invocation, template-independent equivalent and overrides this key when both are set.

Full walkthrough: templates.md.

docs.title: Environment variables and dotenv
docs.text:
Most ffleet.toml keys have an environment-variable equivalent, and Forge Fleet also loads a dotenv file from the current working directory if present. An env var (or dotenv entry) overrides the matching ffleet.toml key; a CLI flag overrides both (see config precedence).

Dotenv discovery order in the current working directory (only the first existing file is loaded):

  1. .env.forge-fleet
  2. .forge-fleet/.env

Env var mapping:

Identity (project_name, source_dir, worktree_root) is config-only: it is read straight from ffleet.toml and has no env-var or CLI-flag override. Run ffleet init to create the config; without it, the env commands fail with a no ffleet config found — run 'ffleet init' error.

Env var Maps to SLUG slug positional argument IMAGE_NAME --image CODING_AGENT --coding-agent (on up; set only when first creating an env). The legacy AGENT / --agent names still work, each with a one-time deprecation notice. CLAUDE_DIR --claude-dir CLAUDE_AUTH --claude-auth (auto, keychain, token, api-key, credentials-file, external) CODEX_DIR --codex-dir UV_CACHE_DIR --uv-cache-dir EXTRA_MOUNTS --extra-mounts (source:target,source:target) EXTRA_HOSTS --extra-hosts (host:address,host:address; each becomes a docker run --add-host, e.g. host.docker.internal:host-gateway) DOCKER_ENV_FILE --docker-env-file GIT_MODE --git-mode (auto, off, worktree, clone) GIT_LOCAL_MAIN local-branch mode when first creating an env (true/false) DOCKER_HOST_BIND --docker-host-bind (true/false) GIT_ALLOW_ORIGIN_WRITES deny the agent outward-facing git/gh commands when false (true/false); no CLI flag equivalent GIT_HTTPS_REWRITE rewrite git remotes to HTTPS inside the container (true/false); no CLI flag equivalent ATTACH ffleet up's attach default (true/false); --attach / --no-attach override it, and -y forces no-attach unless --attach is given FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_NAME explicit git identity name override FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_EMAIL explicit git identity email override LINEAR_API_KEY Linear personal API key, read directly when pm = "linear"; no CLI flag equivalent

A leading ~ in CLAUDE_DIR, CODEX_DIR, UV_CACHE_DIR and DOCKER_ENV_FILE is expanded to your home directory at startup — these vars are exported to every process Forge Fleet starts, including the shell ffleet goto drops you into, so they must hold real paths.

Example .env.forge-fleet:

IMAGE_NAME=forge-fleet:latest
CODING_AGENT=claude
CLAUDE_DIR=~/.claude
CODEX_DIR=~/.codex
UV_CACHE_DIR=~/.cache/uv
EXTRA_MOUNTS=~/.agents:/home/buddy/.agents
DOCKER_ENV_FILE=/path/to/docker.env
GIT_MODE=auto
DOCKER_HOST_BIND=false
FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_NAME=Jane Developer
FORGE_FLEET_GIT_USER_EMAIL=jane@example.com
# Only needed when pm = "linear":
LINEAR_API_KEY=lin_api_xxxxxxxx

EXTRA_MOUNTS format rules:

  • comma-separated entries: <source>:<target>[:ro|:rw]
  • source supports ~ expansion
  • relative source is resolved from the current working directory
  • target must be an absolute container path (start with /)
  • an optional trailing :ro or :rw sets the mount mode (default is read-write); any other trailing segment is rejected
  • entries are bind-mounted as -v <source>:<target> (read-write) or -v <source>:<target>:ro (read-only)
  • if an extra mount uses the same target as an existing mount, the later extra mount can shadow the earlier one

docs.title: Config discovery order
docs.text:
For a given directory, Forge Fleet locates the ffleet.toml to use in this order:

  1. an explicit config path (FFLEET_CONFIG env var)
  2. an explicit project config dir (FFLEET_PROJECT_DIR env var)
  3. the ~/.forge-fleet/registry.json lookup by the directory's project id
  4. legacy in-repo search: ffleet.toml, then .forge-fleet/ffleet.toml

The project id is derived from git structure — the main checkout's git rev-parse --git-common-dir plus its origin remote, or a path hash when there is no remote — never from the current directory's name. That's why every worktree of a project resolves to the same config.
